[p-154] (Sūrat al-Isrā' is Meccan, except verses 26, 32, 33, 57, and from verse 73 to verse 80, which are Medinan. Its number of verses is one hundred and eleven.)

﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾. *Subḥāna* is a proper noun (ʿalam) for glorification, like ʿUthmān as a man's name. Since the named thing is a meaning and not a concrete entity, and a genus and not a particular person, its genitive construction (*iḍāfa*) is not of the type found in *Zayd al-Ma'ārik* or *Ḥātim Ṭayyi'*. Its accusative case (*naṣb*) is governed by a verb that is omitted from speech; its implied form is "I glorify God, the Glory of..." etc. In it there is what is not hidden of a powerful indication of transcendence (*tanzīh*), in terms of its derivation from *al-sabḥ*, which is going off and moving away across the earth; from it comes the phrase *faras sabbūḥ*, meaning a horse with wide gallop. It also has the aspect of transferring (*naql*) to the *tafʿīl* form, and the aspect of shifting from the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) to a noun specifically assigned to this meaning, especially since it is a proper noun that points to a reality present in the mind, and the aspect of its standing in place of the verbal noun together with the verb. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun like *ghufrān*, meaning "transcendence." Thus there is emphasis in attributing transcendence to His sacred essence, and a complete correspondence between the omitted element and what is coordinated with it in His words, exalted is He, "and exalted," as if it were said: "He transcended by His essence and was exalted."

*Al-isrāʾ* is traveling by night specifically, like *al-surā*. His words ﴿by night﴾ serve to indicate the brevity of the time of the night journey, because of the indefiniteness in it, which indicates partiality with respect to parts, just as it indicates partiality with respect to individuals. For when you say "I traveled at night," it indicates that the time of your journey is part of the nights, just as it indicates that it is part of one individual night. This differs from when you say "I traveled the night," which indicates that the travel encompassed the whole night, so that it is a measure of the travel and not a container for it. This is supported by the reading *min al-layl*, meaning "part of the night."

The choice of the word "servant" (*ʿabd*) is to announce that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was wholly devoted to the worship of God, exalted is He, and that he reached in that the utmost extremity and the farthest final point, as the beginning and end of the night journey suggest. The attribution of transcendence, or of transcending, to the relative pronoun mentioned indicates that what is in the clause of the relative (*ṣila*) is the cause for the thing attributed; for that is among the proofs of the perfection of His power, the excess of His wisdom, and the ultimate of His transcendence above the attributes of created beings.

﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾. There has been disagreement about the starting point of the journey. It has been said that it is the Sacred Mosque itself, and this is the apparent meaning, for it is narrated from him, upon him be blessings and peace, that he said: "While I was in the Sacred Mosque, in the Ḥijr beside the House, between sleeping and waking, Gabriel, upon him be blessings and peace, came to me with the Burāq." It has also been said that it is the house of Umm Hānī bint Abī Ṭālib. The meaning of "the Sacred Mosque" is the Sacred Precinct (*al-Ḥaram*), because it encompasses the mosque and is connected to it, or because the whole Sacred Precinct is a mosque. For it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: "He, upon him be blessings and peace, was sleeping in the house of Umm Hānī after the night prayer, and what happened happened, and he related it to her. When he rose to go out to the mosque, she clung to his garment to prevent him, fearing that the people would deny him. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'Even if they deny me.' When he went out, Abū Jahl sat down with him, and he, upon him be blessings and peace, informed him of the hadith of the night journey. Abū Jahl said: 'O assembly of Kaʿb ibn Lu'ayy ibn Ghālib, come!' [p-155] So he related it to them. Some clapped and some placed their hands on their heads in wonder and denial, and some of those who had believed in him apostatized. Some men went to Abū Bakr and said: 'If he said that, then he has spoken the truth.' They said: 'Do you affirm him in that?' He said: 'I affirm him regarding what is even further than that.' Therefore he was named *al-Ṣiddīq* (the Truthful). There were among them those who knew Bayt al-Maqdis, so they asked him to describe the mosque, and it was made manifest to him, and he began to look at it and describe it to them. They said: 'As for the description, he has hit upon it.' Then they said: 'Tell us about our caravan.' So he informed them of the number of its camels and their conditions, and said: 'It will arrive on such-and-such day at sunrise, led by a grey-brown camel.' So they went out running on that day toward the mountain pass. One of them said: 'By God, this is the sun that has risen.' Another said: 'By God, this is the caravan that has come, led by a grey-brown camel, just as Muḥammad said.' Then they did not believe. May God fight them; how are they deluded?'"

Its time has also been disputed: it has been said that it was one year before the Hijra. It is narrated from Anas and al-Ḥasan that it was before the prophethood (*baʿtha*). Also disputed is whether it was in wakefulness or in a dream. From al-Ḥasan it is narrated that it was in a dream, but most of the reports are contrary to this. The truth is that it was in a dream before the prophethood, and in wakefulness after it.

It is also disputed whether it was bodily (*jismānī*) or spiritual (*rūḥānī*). From ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, it is narrated that she said: "The body of the Messenger of God was not lost, but he was taken up with his spirit." From Muʿāwiya it is narrated that he said: "It was only his spirit that was taken up." The truth is that it was bodily, as is indicated by the opening with transcendence and by what is contained in it of wonder, for the spiritual does not entail such astonishment, denial, and breaking of custom to this degree. For this reason Quraysh wondered at it and deemed it impossible. There is no impossibility in it, for it has been established in geometry that the diameter of the sun is more than a hundred and sixty times the diameter of the earth. Then its lower edge reaches the position of its upper edge through the motion of the greatest sphere, together with the resistance of the motion of its own sphere to it, in less than a second. It has been established that bodies are equal in receiving accidents, of which motion is one, and that God, exalted is He, is capable of everything that falls within the scope of possibility. So He is able to create motion like that, indeed faster than it, in the body of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, or in what carries him. Had it not been considered extraordinary, it would not have been a miracle.

﴿to the Farthest Mosque﴾, that is, Bayt al-Maqdis. It was named so because at that time there was no mosque beyond it. In that there is an evocation of the meaning of transcendence and of wonder, which is not hidden.

﴿the one around which We have blessed﴾ with the blessings of religion and of the world, because it is the place of descent of revelation and the place of worship of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace.

﴿that We may show him﴾ is the purpose (*ghāya*) of the night journey, ﴿of Our signs﴾, the great ones, among which is his going in a fraction of the night a distance of a month's journey. That is not harmed by the fact that this was before reaching the destination, and by witnessing Bayt al-Maqdis, and by the appearance of the prophets to him, and his standing at their lofty stations, upon them be blessings and peace. The shift to the first person plural (*iltifāt ilā al-takallum*) is to magnify those blessings and signs. It is also read *liyurayahu* with a *yāʾ*.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing﴾ of his words, upon him be blessings and peace, without ears,

﴿the All-Seeing﴾ of his deeds without eyes, as the restriction (*qaṣr*) indicates, so He honors him and brings him near according to that. In this there is a hint that the mentioned night journey was only for honoring him, upon him be blessings and peace, and elevating his rank; otherwise, comprehension of his words and deeds is attained without any need for bringing near. The shift to the third person (*iltifāt ilā al-ghayba*) is to cultivate awe.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 2:

﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah. In this there is an allusion to his (peace be upon him) being summoned to Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and to the private conversation (munajah) that took place there, combining the two matters which are united in meaning. Here the ascent of the Prophet (ﷺ) to the heavens is not mentioned, nor what took place in it, the reality of which cannot be fully grasped, as expressed in Surat al-Najm, in order to bring the Night Journey (al-Isra') closer to the acceptance of the listeners. That is: We gave him the Torah after We had caused him to travel by night to Mount Sinai.

﴿And We made it﴾, that is, that Book, ﴿a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾, by which they would be guided through what is within its contents.

﴿That you not take﴾, that is, "do not take", like the phrase "I wrote to him that he should do such-and-such" (kataba ilayhi an af'ala kadha). It is also read with the ya' (yattakhidhu, "that they not take"), in which case "an" is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and the meaning is: We gave Moses the Book for the guidance of the Children of Israel, so that they would not take ﴿besides Me a Disposer of affairs﴾, that is, a lord upon whom you rely for your affairs. The singular form (wakilan) is used because fa'il (wakil) is singular in form but collective in meaning.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 17, verse 3:**

﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ is in the accusative by way of specification (*ikhtisas*, a grammatical construction that singles out a noun for mention), or by way of address (*nida'*, vocative), on the reading of the prohibition. The purpose is to emphasize the command to affirm monotheism by reminding them of God's favor to them, implicit in the rescue of their forefathers from the flood in Noah's ship, peace be upon him. Alternatively, it is one of the two objects of *لا يَتَّخِذُوا* (*la yattakhidhu*, "that they not take") on the reading of negation, and *مِن دُونِي* (*min duni*, "other than Me") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) modifying *وَكِيلًا* (*wakilan*, "guardian"). This is like His saying, ﴿Nor would He order you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾.

It was also read in the nominative, either as the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtada' mahdhuf*), or as an apposition (*badal*) from the *waw* of *لا تَتَّخِذُوا* (*la tattakhidhu*, "do not take"), replacing the apparent noun for the pronoun of address, as is the view of some of the Baghdadi grammarians (*al-baghdadah*). It was also read as *ذِرِّيَّةَ* (*dhirriyyata*) with a kasra on the dhal.

﴿Indeed he﴾, that is, Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿was a grateful servant﴾, abundantly thankful in all his circumstances. In this there is an indication that the rescue of those with him came through the blessing of his gratitude, peace be upon him, and an exhortation to his offspring to follow his example, and a warning to them against polytheism, which is the greatest degree of ingratitude. It has been said that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 4:**

﴿And We decreed﴾ i.e., We completed and decided, sending down [the decree].

﴿to the Children of Israel﴾ i.e., revealing to them ﴿in the Book﴾ i.e., in the Torah. For the sending down and the revelation to Musa (peace be upon him) is a sending down, and a revelation to them.

﴿You will surely cause corruption on the earth﴾ is the answer to an implied oath (qasam mahdhuf), and it is permissible to treat the decree that is binding (al-qada' al-mahtum) as occupying the place of an oath, as if it were said: "And We swore that you will surely cause corruption."

﴿twice﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar), and the governing element of it is of a different kind from it (min ghayr jinsihi). The first of them: opposing the ruling of the Torah, the killing of Sha'ya (peace be upon him), and the imprisonment of Irmiya when he warned them of the wrath of Allah, exalted is He. The second: the killing of Zakariyya and Yahya, and the intent to kill 'Isa (peace be upon them all).

﴿and you will surely become exceedingly arrogant﴾ you will be arrogant toward obedience to Allah, glorified is He, or you will overpower the people through oppression and transgression, and you will go to excess in that, exceeding all bounds.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 17, verse 5:

﴿So when the promise of the first of them came﴾ That is: the first of the two times of corruption, meaning the time arrived for the punishment that had been promised to fall.

﴿We sent against you﴾ to take you to account for your crimes, ﴿servants of Ours﴾. It is recited as (ʿabīdan lanā) عَبِيدًا لَنا, with the word ʿabīd in place of ʿibād. ﴿possessors of great might﴾, that is, possessors of strength and forcefulness in war. They were Sanjarib (Sennacherib) of the people of Nineveh and his soldiers. It is said that they were Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar), an agent of Lohrasp. It is also said that they were Jalut (Goliath).

﴿And they went through﴾, that is, they roamed seeking you out with corruption. It is recited with the letter ḥāʾ, فَجاحُوا, and the meaning is the same. It is also recited as (wa-jūsū) وَجُوسُوا.

﴿between the homes﴾, in their midst, for killing and raiding. It is recited as (khilala al-diyar) خِلَلَ الدِّيارِ. They killed their scholars and elders, burned the Torah, destroyed the Temple, and took seventy thousand of them captive. This was part of the practice of God, by which some wrongdoers are made to rule over others, (p-157) which is the divine custom that has been followed.

﴿And it was﴾ that ﴿a promise to be fulfilled﴾, without doubt, in such a way that nothing can turn it aside and nothing can change it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 6:

﴿Then We gave you back the return [of victory] over them﴾, that is, the dominion and the upper hand, ﴿over them﴾, over those who did to you what they did after a hundred years, when you repented and turned back from the corruption and arrogance you had been engaged in. It was said: this was the killing of Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar), the rescue of the Children of Israel's captives and their wealth, and the return of rule to them. That is because when Bahman ibn Isfandiyar inherited the kingship from his grandfather Kashtasp ibn Lohrasp, God Most High put compassion for them into his heart, so he returned their captives to al-Sham (Greater Syria), and he made Daniel, peace be upon him, their ruler. They then overpowered those among Bukhtnassar's followers who were there. It was also said: this was the killing of Jalut (Goliath) by Dawud, peace be upon him.

﴿And We aided you with wealth﴾, abundant, after your wealth had been plundered, ﴿and sons﴾, after your children had been taken captive, ﴿and We made you more numerous in manpower (nafir)﴾ than you were before, or more than your enemy. The nafir is the one who goes out with a man from his people. It was also said: it is the plural of nafar, meaning the people gathered to go out against the enemy, such as the slaves and the helpers.

﴿If you do good﴾ in your deeds, whether they are *lāzima* (intransitive, affecting only yourselves) or *muta'addiya* (transitive, extending to others), that is, if you perform them in the proper manner. This cannot be conceived unless the deeds are good in themselves. Or, if you do good, ﴿you do good for yourselves﴾, because its reward belongs to them.

﴿And if you do evil﴾ in your deeds, by performing them not in the proper manner, which entails inherent evil, or if you commit wrongdoing, ﴿then it is for them﴾, since its consequence falls upon them. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "I have never done good to anyone, nor done evil to him," and he recited ﴿Then when the promise of the Last [Time] comes﴾, meaning the time of the punishment for the second transgression has arrived, as He promised.

﴿To disfigure your faces﴾ is connected to a verb omitted because of what preceded it, indicating its meaning. That is, "We sent them so that they might disfigure [your faces]." The meaning of ﴿to disfigure your faces﴾ is that they make the marks of distress and dejection visible on your faces, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The faces of those who disbelieved will be made ugly﴾.

It has been recited as *liyasūʾa* (with the subject being Allah, or the promise, or the sending). It has also been recited as *linasūʾa* with the *nūn* of majesty (the plural of greatness). In the recitation of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, it is *linusawwiʾanna*, taking it as the answer (*jawāb*) to *idhā* ("when"). It has also been recited as *linusawwiʾ* with the light *nūn*, and *liyusawwiʾanna*.

The *lām* in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿and to enter the Masjid﴾ is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*) upon *liyasūʾū*, dependent (*mutaʿallaq*) on what it depends upon, ﴿as they entered it the first time﴾, that is, at the first time. ﴿And to destroy what they had conquered﴾, that is, to ruin what they overcame and seized, or for the duration of their domination ﴿with complete destruction﴾, a dreadful destruction beyond description. This came about when Allah, whose authority is exalted, gave the Persians power over them. The king of Babylon, one of the kings of the Tawā'if (the Parthian/Arsacid rulers), whose name was Jūdardū, invaded them. It is said his name was Jurdūs. It is also said that the commander of the army entered the altar of their sacrifices and found in it blood boiling. He asked them about it, and they said: "It is the blood of a sacrifice that was not accepted from us." He said: "You are not telling me the truth," and so he killed thousands over it, yet the blood did not calm. Then he said: "If you do not tell me the truth, I will leave none of you alive." They said: "It is the blood of Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā, peace be upon them both." He said: "For a thing like this your Lord would take vengeance upon you." Then he said: "O Yaḥyā, my Lord and your Lord knows what befell your people because of you. Be calm, by Allah's permission, before I leave none of them alive." And it calmed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 8:

﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ after the second occurrence, if you repent (p-158) a further repentance and desist from the sins you were engaged in.

﴿But if you return﴾ to the corruption you were in, a second time, ﴿We will return﴾ to punishing you. They did return, so God, glorified is He, restored retribution upon them by setting over them the Persian kings (akasira), and they did to them what they did, such as imposing the tribute (ita'a) and similar things. It is reported from al-Hasan: "They returned, so God, exalted is He, sent Muhammad (ﷺ), and they give the jizya (poll tax) willingly, while they are humbled." It is reported from Qatadah the same.

﴿And We have made Hell a prison (hasir) for the disbelievers﴾, that is: a confinement from which they cannot come out forever and ever. It was also said: a carpet, as a mat (hasir) is spread out. The phrasing deviated from saying "and We have made Hell for you a record" (of your disbelief through returning) and a censure of them for that, and an indication of the cause of the ruling.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 9:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an﴾, which We have bestowed upon you, ﴿guides﴾, that is, guides mankind in its entirety, not a particular group among them, just as the Book which We gave to Musa (Moses) did.

﴿to that which﴾ is to the way which ﴿is most upright﴾, that is, the most upright and straightest of ways, namely the religion of Islam (millah al-Islam) and monotheism (tawhid). The omission of mention of it is not intended as a generalisation of it, nor of the state, nor of the quality, nor of similar terms by which the intended meaning is expressed; rather it is to indicate that there is no need to state it explicitly, because of its utter clarity, especially after the mention of guidance, which is among its companions. Its being guided to it means that it is such that whoever holds fast to it will be guided to it, not the actual attainment of guidance, for that is specific to the believers at that point.

﴿And gives good news to the believers﴾ of what is in its contents of rulings and laws. It is also read with the lighter pronunciation (bi-l-takhfif). ﴿Those who do righteous deeds﴾, which are explained therein, ﴿that for them﴾, that is, that for them, in return for those deeds, ﴿is a great reward﴾, both in its essence and, by way of multiplication, ten times or more.

And as for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, and its rulings set forth therein of resurrection, reckoning and recompense, singling it out for mention from among the rest of what they disbelieved in is because it is the greatest of what they were commanded to believe in, and in order to maintain the correspondence between their deeds and their recompense, which is indicated by the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾, namely the punishment of Jahannam. That is: We have prepared for them, for what they disbelieved in and denied the existence of, of the Hereafter, a painful punishment. It is more effective in deterrence, since the arrival of punishment from where one does not expect it is more dreadful and more distressing. The sentence is conjoined to the sentence "yubashshiru" (gives glad tidings) by supposing a verb "yukhbiru" (informs), or it is conjoined to the statement of the Exalted: "that for them" (inna lahum), included with it under the "glad tidings," which is used figuratively to mean general informing, encompassing informing of good news and, literally, of bad news; so this constitutes an explanation of the guidance of the Qur'an through encouragement and warning. It is also permissible that "glad tidings" retains its own meaning, and what is intended is the giving of glad tidings to the believers of two tidings: their reward, and the punishment of their enemies. And the statement of the Exalted:

﴿And man prays for evil﴾ is an exposition of the state of the misguided after the statement of the state of the guide, and a showing of the contrast between them. By "man" is meant the species. The state of some of its individuals is attributed to it, or its state at some times is related about it. The meaning on the first reading is that the Qur'an calls man to the good, than which there is no greater good in reward, and warns him against the evil, than which there is no greater evil behind it, namely the painful punishment. Some of mankind, namely the disbeliever, prays for himself for what is evil, that is, for the punishment mentioned. He does so either with his tongue literally, like the conduct of those among them who said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the heaven, or bring us a painful punishment﴾, and like the one who said, "Bring upon us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful," and other such things related about them. Or he does so with their evil deeds that lead to it and make it due, metaphorically, as is the habit of all of them.

﴿His prayer for good﴾ means: like his prayer for the good mentioned, supposed rather than actual, for he is far from praying for it. There is in this an allusion that this is what is fitting to his condition. ﴿And man is ever hasty﴾ means: whoever among its individuals is attributed the aforesaid prayer. He hastens to seek whatever occurs to his mind, heedless of its harm, or he is excessive in haste, seeking the punishment, which will certainly come to him. In this there is a kind of mockery of him. If the prayer is taken to refer to their deeds, then haste is taken to mean obstinacy and persistence in incurring punishment through those deeds.

On the second reading: the Qur'an calls man to what is better. In some of his states, such as anger, he leaves it and prays to Allah Most High against himself, his family and his property for what is evil. Man, by his natural constitution, is hasty and impatient, not waiting until what afflicts him passes. It has been related that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, handed over a captive to Sawda, and she loosened his bonds out of mercy for his moaning at night from the pain of the shackle, so he fled. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was informed of this, he said: "O Allah, cut off her hands." Sawda raised her hands, expecting the answer, and he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I asked Allah Most High that my prayer against whoever among my family does not deserve punishment be a mercy." Or he prays for what is evil while thinking it good. Man is hasty, not discerning, not reflecting on his affairs with due reflection, so that he may ascertain what is truly good and deserving of prayer, and what is evil and deserving of seeking refuge from.

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾. This begins the explanation of some aspects of what was mentioned about guidance, namely directing people to the path of reasoning through the signs and the cosmic proofs (al-dalail al-afaqiyya), each of which is a luminous proof with no doubt in it, and a clear method that does not lead astray whoever follows it. The aforementioned "making" and what is conjoined to it, namely the effacing of the sign of the night and the making of the sign of the day visible, although they are among the creational guidances (al-hidayat al-takwiniyya), the report of them is nonetheless among the Qur'anic guidances that alert to those guidances. The night is mentioned first to observe the existential order, since the day emerges from it, and in it the bright beginnings of the months (ghurar al-shuhur) appear. Had the night been attached to the day preceding it, it would belong to one month while its owner would belong to another month. Also, the ultimate purpose of the sign of the day is ordered upon it without intermediary. That is, We made the two luminaries, with their forms, their succession, and their difference in length and shortness, upon a wondrous regularity (watira) in which minds are bewildered in comprehending it, two signs indicating that they have a wise, powerful, all-knowing Maker, and guiding to what the noble Qur'an guided to: the religion of Islam and monotheism.

﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾. The idafa (construct phrase) here may be explicative (bayaniyya), as in the idafa of a number to what is counted. That is, We effaced the sign which is the night. Its benefit is to confirm the content of the preceding clause. Its effacing means making it obliterated and dimmed of light, but not after it had been otherwise; rather, it was originated in that state, as in their saying: "Glory be to the One who made the gnat small and the elephant large," meaning He originated them so. The fa' is explanatory (tafsiriyya), because the aforementioned effacing and what is conjoined to it are not something occurring after the making of the two renewed things as signs; rather, they are part of that making and its completions.

﴿And We made the sign of the day﴾, that is, the sign which is the day in the manner already mentioned, ﴿visible﴾ (p-160), that is, luminous, in which things are seen, described by the state of its people; or visible to people, from "abṣarahu fa-baṣarahu" (he made him see, so he saw). This may be literal, the sign of night and day being their two luminaries. As for the effacing of the moon, it may be its creation obliterated of light in itself, in which case the fa' is as mentioned. Or it may be the decrease of what it received from the sun little by little until it disappears (al-mihaq), in accordance with the meaning of effacing, and the fa' is for sequence. The making of the sun visible is its origination luminous in itself, possessing rays by which dark things appear.

﴿That you may seek﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿And We made the sign of the day﴾, as indicated, that is: and We made it luminous so that you may seek for yourselves in the brightness of the day ﴿bounty from your Lord﴾, that is, provision, since that is not possible at night. In expressing provision as bounty and earning as seeking, and in mentioning the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which signals the gradual bringing to perfection, there is an indication that the servant has no influence in obtaining provision except seeking. Giving is only from God, glorified be He, not by way of obligation upon Him, but as a favor by the judgment of lordship.

﴿And that you may know﴾ is connected to both verbs, namely the effacing of the sign of the night and the making of the sign of the day visible, not to one of them alone, since one alone would not be the basis for the mentioned knowledge. That is, that you may know by the difference between the two renewed things, or their two luminaries in essence with regard to darkness and illumination with their succession, or their motion and positions, and the rest of their conditions.

﴿The number of the years﴾ in which there is a scientific purpose for establishing your religious and worldly interests.

﴿And the reckoning﴾, that is, the reckoning related to the times contained within them: the months, nights, days, and other things to which some of the aforementioned interests are attached. The year itself, in terms of its realization, is among what reckoning encompasses. What counting relates to is a portion of them, and its relation within that to each one of them is not from the aforementioned aspect, namely the aspect of its realization and obtaining from a number of months, each of which is obtained from a number of days, each of which is obtained by a portion of hours, for example. That is the function of reckoning. Rather, insofar as it is a unit of that counted portion, it counts it, that is, exhausts it, without considering the obtaining of a specific thing from it. Its verification is what passed in Surat Yunus: reckoning is the enumeration of what has discrete quantity by repeating its like, in which a certain portion of it obtains a specific limit that has a special name and an independent ruling, as indicated just now. Counting is enumerating by merely repeating its like without anything of that kind being obtained from it. Since the years were not considered to have a specific limit with a special name and independent ruling, number was attached to them, and reckoning was attached to what else, in which obtaining specific ranks was considered, which have special names and independent rulings. The obtaining of number ranks (tens, hundreds, thousands) is a conventional matter that does not avail in obtaining the counted things. The placing of "number" before "reckoning," although the order between their objects in existence and in knowledge is the reverse, is to alert from the outset that the object of reckoning is what lies within the folds of the years of times; or because the knowledge related to the number of years is a summary knowledge of what reckoning relates in detail; or because number, insofar as no other thing is considered obtained from it, as stated, descends from the reckoning in which that is considered to the station of the simple relative to the compound; or because the knowledge related to the first is the highest of ranks, so it was worthy of precedence in the context of favor. And God, glorified be He, knows best.

﴿And everything﴾ which you need in livelihood and in the hereafter, apart from what was mentioned of making night and day two signs, and what follows from it of religious and worldly benefits. It is in the accusative, governed by a verb which His saying ﴿We have detailed it with detailing﴾ explains. That is, We made it clear in the noble Qur'an with eloquent clarity admitting no ambiguity, like His saying: ﴿And We sent down to you the Book as an explanation of everything﴾. Thus its being a guide to what is most upright became manifest in clear manifestation.

(p-161) ﴿And every human being﴾ who is accountable, ﴿We have fastened his bird﴾ to him. That is: his deeds that proceed from him by his own choice, according to what has been decreed for him, as if it flew to him from the nest of the unseen (ghayb) and the perch of destiny (qadar). Or it refers to what falls to him in the eternal apportionment, which occurs in accordance with his deserving in the eternal knowledge, from the saying of them: "the arrow of such-and-such fell to him" (ṭāra lahu sahmu kadhā).

﴿around his neck﴾ is a depiction of the intensity of its adherence and the completeness of its attachment; that is: We have fastened his deed to him such that it never leaves him, rather it clings to him as a necklace or a shackle clings to the neck, never separating from it in any way. It has also been read with a sukūn on the nūn.

﴿And We shall bring forth for him﴾ with the nūn of majesty. It has also been read with the yā', in the active voice, with the pronoun referring to God, the Mighty and Majestic, and in the passive voice with the pronoun referring to the bird, as in the reading yukhrajue from kh-r-j (to come out) ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾ and the raising for reckoning, ﴿a book﴾ inscribed, containing what was mentioned of his deeds, ﴿spread open﴾ (manshūran)... The word "kitāban" is an object of "nukhriju" according to the first two readings, or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the omitted object referring back to the bird; and according to the other two readings it is a circumstantial accusative from the hidden pronoun in the verb, referring to the bird's pronoun.

﴿He will encounter it﴾, that is: the human being will encounter it, or the human will be met by it.

﴿opened﴾ (manshūran): these two are attributes of the book, or the first is an attribute and the second is a circumstantial accusative of it. It has also been read (yalqāhu) from laqītuhu kadhā, meaning: the human being encounters it.

Al-Ḥasan said: A scroll will be unrolled for you, and two angels have been assigned to you, one on your right and one on your left. As for the one on your right, he records your good deeds; as for the one on your left, he records your bad deeds. When you die, your scroll is folded up and placed with you in your grave, until it is brought out for you on the Day of Resurrection.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 14:**

﴿Read your record.﴾ That is, saying to you, "Read it." It is reported from Qatada: "On that Day, whoever did not read in the world will read." It has also been said that the intended meaning of the "record" (kitab) is the soul itself, imprinted with the traces of its deeds, for every deed a human being performs, whether good or evil, produces in the essence of his soul a specific effect, except that it remains hidden as long as the soul is attached to the body, occupied with the perceptions of the senses and the faculties. When its connection to the body is severed, its resurrection takes place, because the soul had been dwelling and settled within the body. At that point it rises and turns toward ascent to the higher world, the veil is removed, the states are uncovered, and upon the tablet of the soul appears the imprint of everything it did during the span of its life. This is the meaning of writing and reading.

﴿Sufficient is your own soul against you today as a reckoner.﴾ That is, "your soul suffices," with the "ba'" (bi) being superfluous (za'ida), "today" being a time adverbial (zarf) governing "sufficient" (kafa), and "as a reckoner" (hasiban) being a specification (tamyiz), with "against" ('ala) being its complement (silah). This is because it carries the meaning of "the one who reckons," like "sarim" in the sense of "sarim" (the sharp one), from "hasaba 'alayhi kadha" (he reckoned such-and-such against him). Or it carries the meaning of "sufficient" (kafi), and it is placed in the position of "witness" (shahid), because it suffices the claimant in whatever concerns him. Its masculine form is used because what is mentioned, namely reckoning and sufficiency, is among the things typically undertaken by men; or because it is constructed upon interpreting "soul" (nafs) as "person" (shakhs), on the basis that it is an expression for the masculine self, as in the verse of Jabala ibn Huraith:

؎ O soul, you are delighted with pleasures, so remember. Will remembrance benefit you today?

[Translation of the passage follows.]

﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for [the benefit of] his own soul.﴾ This is a summary (fadhlaka) of what preceded concerning the Qur'an's being a guide to the most upright ways and the attachment of deeds to their doers; that is, whoever is guided by its guidance, knows what is contained in its folds of rulings, and refrains from what it forbids, the benefit of his guidance returns only to his own self (nafs), and does not overstep him to another who has not been guided.

﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ from the path to which it guides him, ﴿goes astray only to his own harm﴾; that is, the burden of his error falls only upon himself, and not upon anyone else who has not engaged in it, such that the deed could be separated from its doer.

﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ is an emphasis of the second clause; that is, no soul that carries a burden bears the burden of another soul, such that the second soul could be freed from its burden and the connection between the agent and his deed be disrupted. Rather, each one of them bears only its own burden. This is a confirmation of the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And every human being We have fastened his bird (of fate) to his neck﴾. As for what is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever intercedes with a good intercession will have a share of it, and whoever intercedes with an evil intercession will have a portion of it﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they lead astray without knowledge﴾, it refers to one bearing another's burden and another benefiting from his good deed or being harmed by his evil deed. In reality, this is a benefit from the good deed of his own self and a harm from his own evil deed, for the recompense of the good and evil deeds which the doer performs is necessarily his. What reaches the one who intercedes is only the recompense of his intercession, not the recompense of the root of the good deed or evil deed itself. Likewise, the recompense of error is confined to the astray. What the misleaders bear is only the recompense of misleading, not the recompense of going astray. The emphasis is specifically attached to the second clause in order to cut off vain hopes, since they used to claim that if they were not upon the truth, the responsibility would fall upon their forefathers who had imitated them.

﴿And We would not be punishing﴾ is a statement of divine care following the explanation that the effects of guidance and error are specific to their people, and that the guided person is not deprived of the fruits of his guidance, and that a self is not held to account for the crime of another. That is: it is not valid or proper for Us, rather it is impossible within Our sunnah, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom. Or: it was not in Our past judgment and Our prior decree that We would punish anyone from among the people of error and burdens, being content with the dictate of reason.

﴿Until We send﴾ to them ﴿a messenger﴾ who guides them to the truth, deters them from error, establishes proofs, and lays down the laws according to what is within the folds of the Book revealed to him. As for the punishment negated, it is either the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal), as said by Shaykh Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, may Allah have mercy on him, and this is the one that fits what follows it; or it is the general category that includes the worldly and the otherworldly, and that is among its instances. In either case, the sending is a limit (ghayah) for the impossibility of its occurrence at its appointed time, not for its non-occurrence absolutely. How could it be otherwise, since the otherworldly punishment cannot occur immediately after the sending, and the worldly punishment also does not take place except after the realization of what necessitates it of wickedness and disobedience? Do you not see how the calamity that befell the people of Noah was delayed from them for about a thousand years? And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 16:

﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾ explains how the punishment occurs after the sending of the messenger (al-ba'tha), which was made the limit (ghaya) of its impossibility. By "intention" (al-irada) is not meant its actual realization, since what is intended is not separated from it, nor the eternal intention (al-irada al-azaliyya) related to the occurrence of the intended thing at its appointed time, since the consequent punishment does not coincide with it but rather with the approach of its time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, meaning: when the time of the connection of Our intention with destroying a town draws near, by punishing its people with what We have mentioned of the punishment of extirpation (al-isti'sal), which We have shown cannot be issued by Us before the sending of a messenger, or with a kind of what We have mentioned, its matter being absolute punishment, namely the punishment of extirpation, because of the wrongdoing and sins they have committed, a nearness required by wisdom, without its having a specific fixed limit.

﴿We command﴾ through the messenger sent to its people. ﴿Its affluent ones (mutrafiha)﴾ its pampered ones, its tyrants (jabbarìhā), and its kings. He singled them out for mention even though the command is directed to all, because they are the foundations (al-usul) in address, and the rest are followers of them. And because the directing of the command toward them is more emphatic. The absence of mention of what is commanded (al-ma'mur bihi) is either because it is evident that what is meant by it is the truth and the good, since God does not command indecency, especially after the mention of the guidance of the Qur'an toward what it guides to; or because what is meant is that the command was issued by us, as one says: "So-and-so gives and withholds."

﴿So they defied therein﴾ meaning: they went out of obedience and rebelled.

﴿So the word became due against it﴾ meaning: its requirement was established and realized through the descent of punishment, following what appeared from them of defiance and transgression.

﴿So We destroy it with destruction (tadmiran)﴾ with the destruction of its people, a destruction whose reality cannot be fathomed and cannot be described. This is what is appropriate to what preceded. It has been said: the command is a metaphor for impelling them toward defiance and being the cause of it, by pouring upon them what made them insolent and led them to wickedness. It has been said: it means multiplication; one says "amartu al-shay'a fa-umira," meaning I multiplied the thing so it multiplied. In a hadith: "The best wealth is a well-tended (sikka ma'bura) date-palm row and a fertile (muhra ma'mura) mare," meaning abundant in offspring. This is supported by the reading ﴿آمرنا﴾ (amarna) and ﴿أمرنا﴾ (ammarna), from the form of if'al and taf'il. Both have also been taken from imara (rule), meaning: We made them rulers. But none of this is supported by the context of deterring from misguidance and urging toward guidance, for its implication is that their rebellion is contingent upon the will of God, the Exalted, and His bestowing upon them abundant blessings which made them insolent and drove them to defiance, in a literal sense such that it would be expressed by the command to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 17:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed﴾, i.e., and many a time have We destroyed ﴿from the generations﴾. This is an explanation of "how many" (kam) and a specification (tamyiz) for it. The "qarn" (generation) is a period of time in which a people is cut off (by death), and it is twenty, or thirty, or forty, or eighty, or a hundred years. This is supported by the fact that he (ﷺ) (peace and blessings be upon him) prayed for a man, saying: "Live a qarn," and he lived a hundred years, or a hundred and twenty.

﴿after Noah﴾, i.e., after his time (peace be upon him), such as ʿAd, Thamud, and those after them, among those whose circumstances are narrated in the Great Qur'an, and those whose stories are not narrated. The fact that the people of Noah (peace be upon him) are not mentioned in those destroyed generations is because their matter was manifest; and his (peace be upon him) mention is a symbol of their mention.

﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾, i.e., your Lord is sufficient.

﴿as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants﴾: He encompasses their outward and inward aspects, and so He punishes them for them. The mention of "al-Khabir" (the All-Aware) first is due to the priority of its object, namely the beliefs and intentions which are the origins of the outward actions; or due to its generality, since it also relates to things not seen. In this there is an indication that the sending of messengers, the command, and what follows them, along with their wickedness, is not for acquiring knowledge of the sins that proceeded from them, since that is already obtained before that; rather it is for cutting off excuses and establishing the proof from every aspect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 18:

﴿Whoever desires﴾ by his deeds that he performs, whether the attaining of what is desired by them is by way of recompense, as with deeds of righteousness, or by way of the ordering of effects upon causes, as with means, or with deeds of the Hereafter. So the meaning of "the one who desires" according to the first is the disbelievers and most of the wicked (al-fasiqah). According to the second, it is the people of showing-off (riya') and hypocrisy (nifaq), and the one who emigrates for the sake of the world (dunya), and the one who fights (jihad) solely for the sake of booty (ghanimah).

﴿the fleeting one﴾ only, without desiring the Hereafter along with it, as indicated by the continuity (istimrar) derived from the addition of kana here together with the restriction to the bare act of desiring in its counterpart. The meaning of "the fleeting one" (al-'ajilah) is the worldly abode (al-dar al-dunya). Desiring it means desiring what it contains of the various kinds of its aims, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever desires the tillage of this world﴾. It is also permissible that the fleeting life be meant, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾, but the first is more suitable with His saying: ﴿We hasten for him therein﴾, i.e., in that fleeting abode, for life and its continuance are among what is hastened for him. Therefore the word "man" (man) is more suitable for this, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We shall give him of it﴾ ﴿what We will﴾, i.e., what We will to hasten for him of its bliss, not everything that he desires.

﴿for whomever We will﴾ to hasten what We will for him. It is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "for him", by repeating the preposition, a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd), since it refers back to the relative pronoun which indicates plurality. It was also read as (for whomever He wills), with the pronoun referring to God, glorified is He. It has been said that it refers to "man", so it is specified by "man" and he intends by it that, and he is one of the common people. The restriction of the hastened and the one for whom it is hastened by what has been mentioned of will and desire is because the wisdom upon which the sphere of creation revolves does not require every seeker's reaching his goal, nor every attainer's fulfilling completely what he seeks. As for what appears from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We shall pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they therein will not be deprived﴾, of every hopeful man's attaining all his hopes and every worker's reaching the outcome of his deeds, the discussion of its verification has been indicated in Surah Hud, by the grace of God, exalted is He. ﴿Then We make for him﴾ in place of what We hastened for him ﴿Gehenna﴾, and the kinds of punishment therein ﴿he will burn in it﴾, i.e., enter it. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive, or from Gehenna, or a resumptive sentence (isti'nafi).

﴿blameworthy, rejected﴾, expelled from the mercy of God, exalted is He. It has been said: the verse concerns the hypocrites, who used to show off to the Muslims and fight with them, and their aim was nothing but sharing in the spoils and the like. What rejects this is what is said, that the surah is Meccan except for certain specified verses.

﴿And whoever desires﴾ the Hereafter with his deeds, meaning the Hereafter abode and the lasting bliss it contains, ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾. That is, the striving fitting for it, which is carrying out what was commanded and refraining from what was forbidden, not seeking nearness to God through what they devise by their own opinions. The benefit of the lam in "for it" (lahā) is to take intention (niyyah) and sincerity (ikhlas) into account.

﴿And he is a believer﴾, with a sound faith that is not mixed with anything that undermines it. Introducing faith with a circumstantial clause indicates that it must accompany what was mentioned in the relative clause.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring back to the relative pronoun, by way of the description of being characterized by what is in the relative clause. The sense of distance in it indicates the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station. The plural form observes the meaning, implying that the reward understood from the predicate occurs collectively, that is, to those who combine the praiseworthy traits mentioned: desiring the Hereafter, striving for it in its fitting manner, and faith. ﴿Their striving is appreciated﴾, meaning accepted by God Most High in the best acceptance and rewarded for it. In attaching being appreciated to striving rather than to its two companions, there is an indication that striving is the mainstay of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 20:

﴿Kullan﴾ The tanwin here is a substitute (ʿiwad) for the genitive noun that is added to (al-mudaf ilayhi), meaning: each one of the two groups, not only the last group, the one who desires the good and deserves to be assisted alone.

﴿Numiddu﴾ That is, We increase them time after time, such that the later is an increase (madad) for the earlier. What the increase consists of is the hastened gifts that are given in this world to one of them, and the gifts prepared for the other, the deferred gifts, which are indicated by the fact that their effort is appreciated (bi-mashkuriyyat al-saʿy). That it was not stated explicitly is because of relying on what was previously stated, both explicitly and allusively, and depending on what follows in expression and allusion, as you will see. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ha'ulaʾ﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿kullan﴾, and ﴿wa-ha'ulaʾ﴾ is conjoined to it (ʿatf), meaning: We increase these, those to whom the hastened [gifts] are given, and these, those whose effort is appreciated. The demonstrative refers to the very thing indicated, with what it has of designation, not merely to the essence alone, as the pronoun does. Thus it reminds of what the increase consists of, and specifies the omitted genitive noun to ward off the assumption that it refers to the individuals of the last group, and as an emphasis on the restriction (qasr) derived from the fronting of the object (taqdim al-maful) (p-165). And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿min ʿata'i rabbika﴾ means: from His bestowal, which is vast and has no end, is connected to ﴿numiddu﴾, and it suffices instead of mentioning what the increase consists of, and it alerts that the increase mentioned is not by way of being merited through striving and action, but purely by bounty.

﴿Wa-ma kana ʿata'u rabbika﴾ That is, whether it was worldly or otherworldly, and it was made explicit to give greater attention to its matter and to indicate that it is the cause of the ruling.

﴿mahzuran﴾ prevented from the one who wants it. Rather, it overflows upon whoever has been decreed for it, according to the requirement of a will founded on wisdom, even if something that calls for prohibition is found in him, such as a disbeliever. This is in the sense of a causal explanation for the inclusion of both groups in the increase. The mention of the title of lordship (rububiyya) in both places is to indicate its being the source of what was mentioned of the increase and of the absence of prohibition.

The phrase ﴿Behold how We have favoured some of them over others﴾ has "how" (kayfa) in the accusative position as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the action). The purpose is to clarify what was mentioned earlier about provision, and to show that giving is not restricted, by drawing attention to the ranks of one of the two kinds of giving so that the reader may infer the ranks of the other. The meaning is: consider with the eye of reflection how We have favoured some of them over others in the worldly gifts We have bestowed on them, so that there is the humble and the exalted, the lame and the able-bodied, the owner and the owned, the wealthy and the destitute. By this you will know the ranks of the deferred rewards and the degrees of superiority among their recipients, by way of using the state of the lower to illustrate the state of the higher. This is what His saying, exalted is He, clarifies: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in distinction﴾, meaning that it and what is in it are greater than their measure, and its true nature cannot be comprehended. How could it be otherwise, when it has been described as "that which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no thought has occurred to the heart of a human being"?

It is also permissible that what is meant by the provision is only the worldly gifts. In that case the restriction (qaṣr) mentioned is taken to remove the false assumption that these gifts are exclusive to the first group. The mention of their desiring them and reaching them, without any statement of the relation between them and the second group, could give the impression that the wanting and reaching are exclusive to the first group. So the meaning is: each of the two groups We provide with worldly gifts, not only those whom We have mentioned as desiring them from the first group, from the bounty of your Lord. The giving of this worldly bounty is not withheld from anyone who desires it or from anyone who desires otherwise. Consider how We have favoured, in that giving, some of each of the two groups over others of them. And "and the Hereafter is greater..." (the verse).

The consideration that this giving is not withheld in relation to the first group is to confirm that the provision includes them, as the majority of scholars held, saying: it is not prevented from anyone, even the disobedient, because of his disobedience. This reading implies that the restriction is to remove the assumption that worldly provision is exclusive to the second group, although nothing earlier in the discourse gives the impression that it applies to them, let alone the impression that it is exclusive to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 22:

﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit down reproved and forsaken.﴾ The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and what is meant by it is his community (ummah). This is of the mode of stirring up and urging (al-tahyij wa'l-ilhab). Or it is addressed to everyone who is fit to be addressed.

﴿Lest you sit down﴾: here the verb is in the subjunctive (bi'l-nasb), as a response (jawab) to the prohibition (nahy). The verb "qu'ud" (sitting down) is used with the meaning of "becoming" (al-sayrurah), from the saying of people: "He sharpened the blade until it became (qa'adat)," as if it had become ruined (kharibah); or it is used with the meaning of "incapacity" (al-ajz), from "qa'ada 'anhu," i.e., he was unable to do it.

﴿Reproved and forsaken﴾: these are two predicates (khabarani) or two circumstantial states (halan), meaning: gathering upon yourself blame (al-dhamm) from the angels and the believers, and abandonment (al-khidlan) from Allah, exalted is He. In it is an indication that the one who affirms the oneness of God combines praise and support.

(p-166) ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾, i.e., He has issued a firm command. It was also read: "wa-awṣā rabbuka" and "wa-waṣṣā rabbuka" (and your Lord has enjoined). ﴿That you worship not﴾, i.e., that you not worship ﴿except Him﴾. Here "an" (that) is a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah), and "lā" is a negation; or it is interpretive (mufassirah, "that"), and "lā" is a prohibition (nāhiyah), i.e., "do not worship." This is because worship (ʿibādah) is the utmost degree of glorification, so it is due only to one who possesses the utmost greatness and the highest degree of bounty. This is, as it were, an elaboration of the striving for the Hereafter.

﴿And to parents﴾, i.e., and that you do good to them, or: and do good to them.

﴿Good treatment﴾, because they are the apparent cause of existence and of livelihood.

﴿If one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. "Immā" is composed of the conditional "in" and the redundant "mā," which is added for emphasis; for this reason the energetic nūn (nūn al-tawkīd) has entered the verb. The meaning of "ʿindaka" is: in your care and guardianship. Placing it before the object, although its proper place is after it, is for the sake of building anticipation for its arrival, since it is the source of multiplied care and kindness. "Aḥaduhumā" is the subject of the verb; it is postponed after the adverbial phrase and the object so that the sentence does not become long with it and with what is conjoined to it. It was also read: "yablughān," so "aḥaduhumā" is a substitute (badal) for the dual pronoun, and "kilāhumā" is conjoined to it. There is no way to make "kilāhumā" a corroborative (taʾkīd) of the pronoun. The pronoun of address in "ʿindaka" and in what follows is singular, although what preceded was plural, in order to avoid ambiguity of the intended meaning, since the purpose is the prohibition of every individual from saying "uff" to his parents or scolding them. Had the plural been matched with the plural, or with the dual, this aim would not have been achieved.

﴿So do not say to them﴾, i.e., to either of them, in both states: when alone and when together.

﴿"Uff"﴾: it is a sound that expresses annoyance, or a verb-like noun meaning "I am annoyed." It was read with a kasra without tanwīn, and with a fatḥa or ḍammah both with and without tanwīn. That is: do not show annoyance by it, do not find them repugnant, and do not find their burdens heavy. By this prohibition, the prohibition of all other things that harm them is understood by the indication of the text (dalālat al-naṣṣ). The prohibition was specially mentioned for some of it, to show concern for its matter. Then it is said: ﴿And do not rebuke them﴾, i.e., do not drive them away from what does not please you with harshness. It is said: "nahy," "nahr," and "nahm" are siblings (similar in meaning).

﴿And speak to them﴾ instead of the "uff" and the rebuke, ﴿a generous word﴾: possessing generosity; or it is a description of it by the description of its speaker, i.e., a word issuing from generosity and gentleness. It is the good speech that good manners require and that nobility of character demands, such as saying: "O father," "O mother," as Abraham, peace be upon him, said to his father: "O my father" (yā abatī), despite the disbelief that was in him. And one should not call them by their names, for that is coarseness, bad manners, and the habit of the rowdy. Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ was asked about dutifulness to parents, and he said: "That you do not rise to serve them out of laziness." It was also said: "That you do not raise your voice over them, nor look at them with disdain, nor let them see from you opposition in outward or inward matters, that you show them mercy while they live, pray for them when they die, and attend to the affairs of their friends after them." On this, the Prophet ﷺ said: "Among the greatest forms of righteousness is that a man keep up the ties of affection with the friends of his father."

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾ is a metaphor for gentleness of manner, modesty, and submissiveness toward them, since their honour is only achieved through this. It is as if it were said: "Lower to them your humble wing." Or the phrase means that humility is given a wing, as Labid said:

؎ And on a day of wind, when I uncovered both the cold and its restraint, when the north wind had taken its reins in its hand.

Here the cold is given reins, and the north wind is given a hand, likening it to a bird that lowers its wing over its chicks to nurture them and out of compassion for them. As for making the lowering of the wing a metaphor for abandoning flight, as al-Qaffal did, this does not suit the context.

﴿out of mercy﴾: out of the abundance of your mercy, your tenderness toward them, and your softness toward them, because they are in need today of the one who was the neediest of God's creation toward them. Do not be content with your mortal mercy; rather, supplicate God for them with His vast and enduring mercy. ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy upon them﴾ with Your worldly and otherworldly mercy, of which guidance to Islam is a part. This does not conflict with their disbelief.

﴿as they brought me up﴾: the particle "al-kaf" (الكاف) is in the accusative position as a description of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a mercy like their raising of me, or like their mercy toward me, since raising is itself mercy. It is also permissible that they both had mercy and raising together, and one of them was mentioned on one side and the other on the other side, as is hinted by the mention of the title "Lordship" at the opening of the supplication. It is as if it were said: "My Lord, have mercy upon them, and be their Lord as they had mercy on me and raised me ﴿when I was small﴾." It is also permissible that the particle al-kaf is causal (لِلتَّعْلِيلِ), meaning: because of their raising me, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾.

He, mighty and majestic, has greatly emphasised the charge concerning them, for He began it by pairing kindness to them with the affirmation of His own oneness, and arranged it in the same thread as the decree concerning them both. Then He narrowed the matter in the matter of their treatment, so that He did not permit even the slightest word that might escape from one who is irritated, despite the many causes of irritation that almost cannot be counted. He concluded it by making His mercy, which encompasses everything, to be likened to their raising of the child.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "God's pleasure lies in the pleasure of the parents, and His displeasure lies in their displeasure." It is also narrated: "The dutiful one may do whatever he wishes, and he will not enter the Fire; and the disobedient one may do whatever he wishes, and he will not enter Paradise."

A man said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "My parents have reached such old age that I now attend to them as they attended to me in childhood. Have I fulfilled their right?" He said: "No, for they used to do that while they loved your remaining alive, and you do that while you wish for their death."

It is narrated that an old man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "This son of mine has much wealth, yet he does not spend any of it on me." Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) descended and said: "This old man has composed verses about his son, the like of which no ear has heard. Ask him to recite them." So the old man recited them, and he said:

؎ I nourished you as an infant, and I nurtured you as a youth; you were growing by what I earned for you, and you were drinking.

؎ When a night constrained you with sickness, I did not spend it except weeping, tossing in restlessness over your illness.

؎ As if I were the one afflicted by what you were afflicted with, and my eyes were pouring out tears.

؎ When you reached the age and the goal to which I had hoped for you to attain.

؎ You made my recompense harshness and roughness, as if you were the benefactor and the one who bestows favour.

؎ Would that, since you did not observe my right as a father, you had acted as a neighbouring stranger would act.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) became angry and said: "You and your wealth belong to your father."

Your Lord knows best what is in your souls, of dutifulness and disobedience (﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾), ﴿if you are righteous﴾, intending uprightness and dutifulness rather than disobedience and corruption. ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that is, those who repeatedly return to Him, the Exalted, from whatever slips occur from them, which humans can hardly ever be free of, ﴿Forgiving﴾ of whatever kind of shortcoming, or harmful act or word, has occurred from them. In this there is what is not hidden of emphasis on the command to observe the rights of the two parents. It is also permissible that it be general to every penitent, and the one who wrongs his parents enters into it as a primary inclusion.

﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾, i.e., the kinsman (dhū al-qurbā) his right. This is an injunction concerning relatives, following the injunction to be good to the two parents. Perhaps the intended ones are the mahram (relatives within the prohibited degrees of marriage), and their right is maintenance (nafaqah), as indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾, for the command concerning these two is necessarily financial assistance. That is: give them their right from what was obligatory in Makkah in the position of zakat (obligatory alms). Likewise the prohibition of tabdhir (wasteful squandering) and of excess in withholding and spending (p-168) is in the same category, for all of these are financial dealings.

﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾ is a prohibition against spending wealth on others who do not deserve it, for tabdhir is scattering in other than its proper place. It is taken from scattering grains and casting them however they fall, without tending to their places. It does not refer to excess in giving to them, for otherwise it would be matched by israf (extravagance), which is exceeding the limit in spending, and He has prohibited that in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and do not extend it fully outstretched﴾. Both are blameworthy.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for the prohibition of extravagance (tabdhir), by explaining that it makes its practitioner "linked in the horn of the devils" (malzuzan fi qarn al-shayatin). The meaning of "brotherhood" (al-ukhuwwa) is complete similarity in every attribute of evil in which there is no good, of which extravagance is one. That is: by what they did of extravagance, they were like the devils. Or it means friendship and companionship: they were their friends and followers in what was mentioned of extravagance and spending on sinful things, for they used to slaughter camels, gamble over them (yatayasarun alayha), and squander their wealth for show-off (al-sum'a) and all else that holds no good, such as boasting (al-mabahi) and frivolous amusements (al-malahi). Or it means association (al-muqarana): that they would be their companions in the Fire, as a warning (ala sabil al-w'id).

﴿And Satan has always been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾ This is part of the justification: that is, he is excessive in denying the blessing of God, the Exalted. This is because his nature is to direct all that God, the Exalted, has given him of powers and capacities to other than that for which they were created, namely various kinds of sins, corruption on earth, misleading people, and driving them to disbelief in God and ingratitude for the blessings overflowing upon them, and diverting these to other than what God, the Exalted, has commanded. The singling out of this attribute from among his other ugly attributes is to indicate that extravagance, which is the diversion of God's blessings to other than their proper use, is a form of ingratitude (kufran), which is the opposite of gratitude (shukr), which is the directing of blessings to that for which they were created. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya) is to signal the perfection of his rebellion, for denying the blessing of the Lord, while lordship is among the powers that call one to gratitude for it, is the utmost ingratitude and the extreme of misguidance and transgression.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 28:

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ means: if there comes upon you a matter that compels you to turn away from those who deserve (your help),  ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ means: because of the lack of provision from your Lord, using the cause (al-musabbab) in place of the effect (al-sabab) [iqamat al-musabbab maqam al-sabab], for the loss of provision is a cause for seeking.

﴿Which you hope for﴾ from Allah, the Exalted, so that you may give to them. The Prophet (ﷺ), whenever he was asked for something he did not have, would turn away from the questioner and remain silent out of modesty. So he was commanded to attend to them with kind speech, lest they be seized by desolation at his (ﷺ) silence. Thus it was said: ﴿Then speak to them a gentle word﴾, easy and soft, and promise them a good promise, from yasara al-amr (the matter became easy), like sa'ida (he was made happy). Or say to them: "May Allah provide for us and for you out of His bounty," in the form of a supplication for them that eases their poverty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 29:

﴿Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it with complete extension﴾. These are two allegorical depictions (tamthil) of restraining the miser and of the extravagance of the wasteful, to deter both of them from these two extremes and to urge them toward the moderation (iqtisad) that lies between them:

Both extremes of the right course in affairs are blameworthy.

Since the ugliness of stinginess (shuhh) accompanies it and is known from the outset, this was taken into account in the depiction through the most ugly of images. And since the peril of extravagance (israf) comes at its end, its ugliness was made clear in its consequence, so it was said: ﴿so that you sit reproached﴾, that is, so that you become blamed before God, before people, and before yourself when you are in need and regret what you have done.

﴿Left destitute﴾: regretful, or cut off with nothing left in your possession, from the word hasar, which is used of a traveler when his journey has exhausted him. As for what has been said, that it was narrated from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "While the Messenger of God ﷺ was sitting, a boy came to him and said: 'My mother asks you to give her a garment (dir'),' and he ﷺ said: 'Come back to us from time to time.' So he went to his mother, and she said to him: 'Say: My mother asks you for the garment you are wearing.' So the Prophet ﷺ entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan and they waited, but he did not come out for the prayer." Then this verse was revealed. This is contradicted by the fact that the surah is Meccan, except for some verses at its end.

Likewise, what has been said: "The Prophet ﷺ gave al-Aqra' ibn Habis one hundred camels, and likewise Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari. Then 'Abbas ibn Mirdas came and recited:

Will you place my plunder and the plunder of the slaves
between Uyaynah and al-Aqra'?

Neither Hisn nor Habis
surpasses Mirdas in an assembly.

I was not below either of them,
and whoever is lowered today will not be raised."

The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Abu Bakr, cut off his tongue from me and give him one hundred camels." They were all among the al-mu'allafah qulubuhum (those whose hearts are being reconciled to Islam). Then this verse was revealed:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for what has preceded, meaning: He widens it for some and restricts it for others, as His will, which follows wisdom, determines. So what burdens you of giving (al-ițafah) that would compel you to turn away from those who ask, or the exhaustion of what is in your hand if you extend it entirely, is only for your own benefit.

﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing.﴾ This is a justification for what came before, meaning: He knows their secrets and their open affairs, so He knows what is in their interests and hidden from them. It is also permissible that what is intended is that extending and restricting are of the command of God, who knows the hidden and the apparent, in whose hand are the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, while the servants are obligated to be moderate. It is also permissible that what is intended is that He, exalted, extends at times and restricts at other times, so follow His way: do not restrict with complete restriction, nor extend with complete extension. And it is permissible that what is intended is that He, exalted, extends and restricts according to His will, so do not extend to one whose provision He has restricted. And this may serve as a preparation (tamhid) for His saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 31:

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty.﴾ That is, for fear of destitution. It has also been read with a kasra on the kha' (khashyata, i.e. khishyata). They used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty, so they were forbidden from this.

﴿We provide for them and for you.﴾ Not you alone. So do not fear destitution, on the basis of your knowledge of your inability to secure their sustenance. This is a guarantee of their provision and a reason (ta'lil) for the aforementioned prohibition, by nullifying what in their assumption necessitates it. The placing of the pronoun referring to the children before the addressees, contrary to what occurs in Surat al-An'am, serves to indicate that they are the原 originators (asalah) in the bestowing of provision; or because the motive for killing there is immediate poverty (imlaq najiz), which is why it was said there "from poverty" (min imlaq), whereas here the poverty is anticipated (imlaq mutawaqqa'), which is why it was said here "for fear of poverty" (khashyata imlaq). It is as if it were said: We provide for them without any of your provision being diminished, so that what you fear would befall you; and We also provide for you, in addition to your provision.

﴿Indeed, their killing has been a great sin.﴾ This is another reason (ta'lil), by explaining that what is forbidden is in itself a grave evil. Al-khit' (خِطْء) means sin and guilt; it is said khati'a khit'an, like atham ithman. It has also been read with a fatha and a sukun, and with two fathas, with the same meaning, like al-hidhr and al-hadhar. It has been said that it means the opposite of what is right (didd al-sawab), and it has been read with a kasra on the kha' and a long vowel, with a fatha and a long vowel, with a fatha and the hamza dropped, and with a kasra and the hamza dropped in the same manner.

﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ by engaging in its near or distant beginnings, let alone engaging in it itself. He forbade approaching it, rather than forbidding it outright, contrary to what preceded. The mention of killing came along for emphasis in prohibiting the act itself, and because approaching it leads to engaging in it. The prohibition of it is placed between the prohibition of killing children and the prohibition of killing a soul whose killing is forbidden in every case, on the basis that it is a killing of children, since it wastes lineages, for whoever's lineage is not established is, in legal terms, dead. ﴿Indeed it was an abomination﴾, a deed of manifest ugliness that exceeds the limit.

﴿And an evil way﴾, that is, how evil a path its path is, for it is the seizing of women's chastity, which leads to the disruption of the affairs of lineages and the eruption of strife. How could it not be? The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the servant commits fornication, faith departs from him and becomes like a canopy over his head; when he stops, it returns to him." He (ﷺ) also said: "The fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer." And on the authority of Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of fornication, for in it are six traits: three in this world and three in the Hereafter. As for those in this world: the loss of radiance, the persistence of poverty, and the shortening of life. As for those in the Hereafter: the wrath of Allah Most High, a bad reckoning, and abiding in the Fire."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 33:

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden⁠—﴾ killing it, by which He has protected it with Islam or with a covenant ﴿except by right.﴾ Except by one of three: disbelief after belief, fornication after being chaste (ihsan), and deliberately killing a protected soul. The exception here is "mufarragh" (an exception from an unstated general object), meaning: do not kill it for any cause except the cause of right; or, they (or it) are in a state of being associated with something among things. It is permissible for it to be an attributive (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: do not kill it with any killing except a killing that is associated with right.
