﴿And whoever is killed wronged﴾ without a right that requires his killing, or that makes it permissible for the killer, to the extent that its permissibility is not considered for anyone other than the killer. For whoever is liable to retaliation (qisas), if he is killed by someone other than the one entitled to qisas, retaliation is taken on behalf of him, and the statement of the guardian, "I ordered him to do that," does not benefit him, unless the order was apparent.

﴿We have certainly given his guardian﴾ to the one who takes charge of his affair from among the heirs, or the ruler when there is no heir, ﴿authority⁠﴾ a power and a control over the killer, to hold him accountable through retaliation, or through blood money (diyah) according to what his crime requires, or a conclusive proof.

﴿So let him not commit excess﴾ — and it is read: "let us not commit excess" ﴿in killing⁠﴾ meaning: the guardian should not commit excess in the matter of killing, by exceeding the prescribed limit, such as by adding mutilation to it, or by killing someone other than the killer from among his relatives, or by killing two in place of one, as the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do, or by killing the killer in a matter of blood money. It is also read in the negative form, for emphasis in conveying the meaning of prohibition.

﴿Indeed, he is ever supported⁠﴾ This is a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition. The pronoun refers to the guardian, in the sense that Allah, exalted is He, has supported him by making retaliation or blood money obligatory for him, and by commanding the rulers to assist him in exacting his right. So let him not seek beyond his right, nor demand more than it, nor step outside the bounds of the command of the Supporter. Or the pronoun refers to the one wrongfully killed, in the sense that Allah, exalted is He, has supported him with what has been mentioned, so his guardian should not commit excess concerning his matter. Or it refers to the one whom the guardian kills wrongly and excessively. The reasoning of the causal clause is clear. It is reported from Mujahid that the pronoun in "let him not commit excess" refers to the first killer, and the reading "so do not commit excess (fa-la tusrifu)" supports this. The two pronouns in the causal clause then refer to the guardian or the one killed. The meaning of "excess" in this case is then the first killer's excess against himself by exposing himself to immediate and deferred destruction, not excess and transgression of limits in killing; that is, he should not commit excess against himself in the matter of killing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves⁠﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 34:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ is a prohibition against approaching it, because of the emphasis mentioned in the prohibition against touching it (p-171), and because such approach leads to it, and as a means to the exception in His words: ﴿except in the best manner﴾. That is, except by the trait and method that is the best of traits and methods, namely preserving it and investing it.

﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾ is a limit (ghayah) on the permissibility of disposing of it in the best manner indicated by the exception (istithna'), not only on the manner mentioned alone.

﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾, whether it was made between you and your Lord or between you and other people. Fulfilling (al-iifa') the covenant and being faithful to it (al-wafa') is carrying out its requirement and observing it. It is hardly ever used except with the preposition bi, to distinguish it from the physical fulfilling (al-iifa' al-hissi), such as fulfilling the measure and the weight.

﴿Indeed the covenant﴾: the noun is expressed in place of a pronoun to show full care for its matter, or because the intended meaning is the covenant in general, which includes the specific covenant that was agreed upon.

﴿will be questioned﴾: that is, questioned about it, with the preposition elided, and the pronoun made a raised implicit pronoun in the passive participle after it was transformed, as in His words: ﴿And that is a day witnessed﴾, meaning a day in which it is witnessed. Its parallel is in His words: ﴿These are the verses of the wise Book﴾, on the view that its original form is "the wise one who speaks it", so the modified noun was removed and the pronoun made implicit in "wise" after it was transformed into a raised pronoun. It may also be takhyil (personification), as if it is said to the covenant: "Why were you broken? Would that you had been fulfilled by him," as a rebuke to the one who breaks it, just as it is said to the buried infant girl: ﴿For what sin was she killed?﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 35:

﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾, i.e., complete it and do not make it deficient.

﴿When you measure﴾, i.e., at the time of your measuring for the buyers. The restriction of the command to this circumstance is because it is then that cheating (tatfif) occurs. As for the time of measuring out to people, there is no need for a command to be just, as the Exalted said: ﴿When they take the measure from people, they take it in full﴾ ... the verse.

﴿And weigh with a balance that is upright﴾. The qistas is the qarastun (steelyard/balance). It has been said: every balance, small or large, is Roman (rumi) and arabicized (mu'arrab). This does not detract from the Arabic of the Qur'an, since arabicized words are integrated into the fabric of Arabic speech. It was also read with a ḍamma on the qaf (qusṭās). ﴿Upright﴾, i.e., the straight, sound scale. Perhaps the reason for being satisfied with its uprightness instead of a command to give full weight is that, when it is upright, injustice is generally unimaginable, unlike with measures, where cheating often occurs even when the instrument is upright. Likewise, being satisfied with giving full measure instead of a command to calibrate it is because full measure cannot be conceived without calibrating the measure; and it was also commanded to be made correct in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And give full measure and full weight with justice﴾.

﴿That﴾, i.e., giving full measure and weighing with the upright balance,

﴿is better﴾ in this world, for it is a trust that makes people eager to deal with you and creates a good reputation among people.

﴿And better in outcome﴾ (ta'wil), the verbal noun from āla, meaning to return; what is meant is the end to which it leads.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 36:**

﴿وَلا تَقْفُ﴾ "And do not follow": do not go after, from *qafa* (to follow) the trail of someone when one follows him. It is also read as *"wa-la taquf"*, from *qāfa athārahu*, meaning to follow his trail. From this comes *al-qāfah* (trackers, those who follow trails), the plural of *al-qā'if* (the tracker).

﴿ما لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ﴾ "That of which you have no knowledge": meaning, do not be one who follows, in speech or action, what you have no knowledge of, like someone who takes a path without knowing that it will lead him to his goal. Those who prohibit following conjecture (*ittibā' al-ẓann*) have used this verse as evidence. Its answer is that the intended meaning of *"al-'ilm"* (knowledge) is the prevailing belief derived from a source, whether that source is decisive (*qaṭ'ī*) or speculative (*ẓannī*). Its use in this sense is widely known and cannot be denied. It has also been said that it is restricted to matters of belief (*al-'aqā'id*). It has also been said that it refers to accusing others (*al-ramy*) and false testimony. The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying supports this: "Whoever accuses a believer of what is not in him, Allah will hold him in *radghat al-khabāl* (the mire of the dead) until he brings out [evidence for what he said]." From this is the verse of al-Kumayt:

"I do not accuse the innocent without a sin,
nor do I follow the chaste women if we are accused."

﴿إنَّ السَّمْعَ والبَصَرَ والفُؤادَ﴾ "Indeed the hearing, the sight, and the heart": it is also read with *fatḥ* on the *fā'* and with the *wāw* converted from a *hamzah* when the *fā'* is dammah.

﴿كُلُّ أُولَئِكَ﴾ (p-172) "Each of those": meaning each one of those organs. They were treated as rational beings (*'uqalā'*), since they are questioned about their conditions and bear witness against their owners. This is so. As for *ulā'ika*, although it is predominantly used for rational beings, since it is a plural noun for *dhā* which includes both groups (rational and non-rational), it has also been used for non-rational beings. The poet said:

"He blamed the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwā,
and life after those days."

﴿كانَ عَنْهُ مَسْؤُولا﴾ "Was questioned about": meaning each of those organs was questioned about itself, with the subject of *kāna* being a pronoun referring to *kull* (each), and likewise the pronoun in the genitive. It has also been permitted that the subject be a pronoun referring to the addressee (*al-qāfī*) by way of *iltifāt* (shift of person), since the apparent form would be "you were questioned about it" (*kunta 'anhu mas'ūlan*). It has been said that the prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa-al-majrūr*) is in the position of the nominative, and that *mas'ūlan* has been predicated of it, justified by the fact that a prepositional phrase cannot be confused with the subject (*mubtada'*), and this is the reason for prohibiting the placing of the agent and what takes its place before the verb. However, al-Naḥḥās reported a consensus (*ijmā'*) on the impermissibility of placing the substitute for the agent before the verb when it is a prepositional phrase. It is also permissible that this be a case of deletion (*ḥadhf*) under the condition of explanation (*tafsīr*): the preposition is deleted from the explained element, and the pronoun returns as a concealed pronoun, as we have mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَوْمٌ مَشْهُودٌ﴾. It is also permissible that *mas'ūlan* be predicated of the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) implied by the verb, and that its agent be the verbal noun, which is the questioning (*su'āl*). "'Anhu" is in the position of the accusative. Ibn Jinni asked Abu 'Ali about the expression *fīka yurghabu* ("in you is desired"), saying: "It is not raised by what follows it, so where is the nominative?" He replied: "The verbal noun." That is, *fīka yurghabu al-raghbah*, with the verbal noun meaning "is done the desiring," as in the expression *yu'ṭī wa-yamna'u* ("he gives and withholds"), meaning he performs giving and withholding. It is also permissible that the subject of *kāna*, or its agent, be a pronoun referring to *kull* with the omission of a genitive construct (*muḍāf*), meaning: "its owner was questioned about it," or "its owner was questioned."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 37:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. The restriction (al-taqyid) serves to add emphasis and to signal that walking upon it is not becoming of one who is arrogant (maraḥ). ﴿Exultantly (maraḥan)﴾: with pride (takabbur), insolence (baṭaran), and self-admiration (ikhtiyalan). It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) placed in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal), meaning: "while being full of exultation," or "you exult with exultation," or "for the sake of exultation." It has also been read with a kasra (mariḥan).

﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾. This is a justification (ta'lil) for the prohibition, and it contains mockery (tahakkum) of the one who struts in self-admiration, and an indication (iydhan) that such conduct is boasting against the earth and haughtiness over it. That is: you will never tear the earth apart by your stamping and the force of your tread. It has also been read with a ḍamma on the rā' (takhruqa).

﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾, which are part of the parts of the earth, ﴿in height﴾, such that it would be possible for you to be arrogant over them. For arrogance only comes from abundance of strength and greatness of body, and both are absent. In this there is also an allusion to what the one who struts does of raising his head and walking on the tips of his toes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 38:

﴿All that﴾ refers to what has been understood, within the mention of the commands and prohibitions, of the twenty-five characteristics.

﴿its evil﴾, meaning what He forbade, and these are twelve characteristics.

﴿is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾: detestable, not approved; or "not willed" by the primary will (al-irada al-awwaliyya), not "not willed" absolutely, because of the decisive proofs that all things occur by His will, glory be to Him. This is the completion of the justification for all the forbidden matters together. The description of them all as merely "hateful," although some of them are major sins, indicates that mere disapproval from Him, exalted is He, is sufficient to make it obligatory to refrain from them. The direction of the reference to the whole, then the specification of some (of them) without directing the reference to them from the start, is because the mentioned part is not mentioned as a whole but in a mixed manner. Within this there is an indication that what is other than it is approved by Him, exalted is He. He did not state this explicitly, signifying that the matter is self-evident. It was also said: the idafa (genitive construction) here is explanatory (bayaniyya), as in the verse of the night and the verse of the day. It is also read: ﴿sayyi'atan﴾ (in the accusative), as the predicate (khabar) of kana, and that refers to what was forbidden among the matters mentioned. ﴿Makruhan﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for sayyi'atan, or an adjective (sifa) for it, carried according to meaning, since it has the sense of sayyi'an (an evil thing), and it has been read so; or it is treated as qualifying a masculine noun understood, i.e., "a hateful matter"; or it is treated as a noun in which the sense of being a descriptive word has ceased. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun hidden in kana, or in the adverbial phrase (zarf), on the basis that it is a qualifying adjective of an evil thing. It is also read: ﴿sayyi'atuhu﴾ (in the plural). It is also read: ﴿sha'nuhu﴾.

﴿That﴾: that is, the directives detailed above.

﴿of what your Lord has revealed to you﴾: that is, part of it, or of the same kind.

﴿of wisdom﴾ (ḥikmah, wisdom, here understood as the knowledge of the sacred law (sharā'i'), or knowing the truth for its own sake and acting upon it). Or it means the firmly established rulings (al-aḥkām al-muḥkamah) which are not open to abrogation (naskh) or corruption (fasād). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that these eighteen verses were on the tablets of Moses, peace be upon him, the first of which is: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god﴾. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything an admonition﴾, and these are the ten commandments in the Torah. The word مِن (min, "of/from") is either connected to أوحى (awḥā, "revealed") with the meaning of partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), or of origin (ibtidā'iyyah). Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl), or of its omitted pronoun in the relative clause (ṣilah), meaning: being from wisdom. Or it is a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun, with the preposition repeated.

﴿And do not set up with Allah another god﴾: the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and what is meant is others besides him, from among those who could conceivably commit the forbidden act. It is repeated to draw attention to the fact that monotheism (tawḥīd) is the starting point of the matter and its endpoint, and that it is the head of all wisdom and its foundation. Whoever lacks it, his knowledge and wisdoms will not benefit him, even if he surpasses the pillars of the sages in them and his forehead touches the clouds of heaven. And upon it is ordered what is the outcome of associating partners, or not, where it is said: ﴿so you will sit reproached and forsaken﴾. And its consequence in the Hereafter is ordered here, so it is said: ﴿you will be thrown into Hell, blamed﴾ by yourself and by others.

﴿rejected﴾: removed from the mercy of Allah the Exalted. The use of the verb "to be thrown" in the passive voice (mabnī lil-mafʿūl) follows the manner of divine majesty and contempt for the polytheist, and makes him like a piece of wood that a person takes in his hand and throws into the oven (tannūr).

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself females from among the angels?﴾ This is addressed to those who claim that the angels are the daughters of God, glorified be He. Isfa' (إصفاء) with something means making it pure and unmixed. The hamzah is for denial, and the fa' is for coordination with an implied premise that the following statement explains. The meaning is: "Has He preferred you over His own essence, so that He singled you out with the most excellent children in a pure form, and chose for Himself the basest and lowliest of them?" This is like His statement, glorified be He: ﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ and His statement, exalted be He: ﴿Or has He daughters while you have sons?﴾ Here, by invoking the title of Lordship, the intention is to intensify and emphasise the denunciation. By mentioning the angels, peace be upon them, and using "females" in place of "daughters," there is an allusion to another kind of disbelief: their description of them, peace be upon them, with femaleness, which is the lowest of the attributes of animals. This is like His statement, exalted be He: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females.﴾

﴿Indeed, you are saying﴾ in accordance with your false doctrine, which is the attribution of offspring to Him, glorified be He, ﴿a grievous saying﴾ whose gravity cannot be measured in the sin it entails and in its violation of the dictates of reason, to the extent that no one would dare to utter it. They make Him, exalted be He, one of the kinds of bodies that are homogeneous and quick to pass away, though "there is nothing like unto Him" (42:11), and He is the One, the Subduer, the Everlasting in His own essence. Then you attribute to Him what you dislike of the basest offspring, and you prefer yourselves over Him with sons, then you describe the angels, who are among the noblest of creatures, with femaleness, which is among the lowest attributes of animals. How strange is such error, how ugly it is, and how monstrous and atrocious is such disbelief! (p-174)

**Verse 41:** ﴿And We have indeed varied this meaning and repeated it﴾ ﴿in this Qur'an﴾ in various forms of variation in its places. The pronoun was omitted only because it is clear from context. It is also read with the lighter (tashdid-free) pronunciation.

﴿That they may take heed﴾ of what is in it, and come to realize the falsity of what they say. The shift to the third person (ghaybah) signals that the situation calls for turning away from them and relating their failings to the listeners. It is also read with the lighter pronunciation, from dhikr, meaning tadhakkur (remembrance). It is also permissible that by "this Qur'an" is meant the noble verses that speak to the falsity of their stated claim, coming in differing styles. The meaning of "variation" (tasrif) in it is making it a place for it, i.e., We placed variation in it, as in the poet's saying: "it wounds in its flanks my blade." It has also been allowed that by it is meant the refutation of their attribution to Him, exalted is He, of daughters, and you know that this refutation is among the effects and results of the Qur'an.

﴿And it increases them﴾ i.e., while the situation is that this extensive variation increases them in nothing,

﴿but aversion﴾ from the truth, and turning away from it, let alone remembrance that leads to knowledge of the falsity of the abominations they hold.

Qul (Say): to make manifest the falsity of that from another angle.

Law kana ma'ahu (If there were with Him) — exalted is He — alihatun (gods) kama yaqulun (as they say): i.e., the polytheists in general. It is also read with the ta' (tu'), addressed to them from the Prophet (ﷺ). The kaf (ka) is in the accusative position, being an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), i.e., "a being similar to what they say." By similarity is meant agreement and correspondence.

Idhan labtaghaw (Then they would have sought) is the answer to their monstrous statement and the apodosis (jaza') of "law" (if), i.e., they would have sought...

Ila dhi al-'arsh (to the Lord of the Throne): i.e., to the One who possesses dominion and lordship absolutely.

Sabilan (a way): by overpowering and resisting, as is the custom of kings with one another, following the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [21:22]. It was also said: by drawing near to Him, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord﴾ [17:57]. The first is the more apparent and more fitting.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 43:

﴿Glory be to Him﴾. This is explicit that the purpose is to show that what they say entails a grave prohibited matter from a direction they do not reckon. As for seeking a way to Him, the Exalted, through drawing near (taqarrub), this is not something specific to this explanation, nor is it among the things that would follow for them without their awareness. Rather, it is a matter they believe outright. That is, He is exalted in His essence with a true exaltation befitting Him.

﴿And exalted is He﴾, far removed ﴿from what they say﴾ of the great falsehood, which is that there are gods with Him and that He has daughters.

﴿Exalted, highly exalted﴾ (ʿulūwan kabīran), like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾, ﴿great﴾, with no limit beyond it. How could it not be so? He, glory be to Him, is at the furthest ends of existence, which is necessary existence in His essence (al-wujub al-dhati). What they say, that He has partners and offspring, lies at the most distant levels of non-existence, namely impossibility (al-imtina'), not because He, the Exalted, is at the highest levels of existence, which is His being necessarily existent through His essence (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi). Taking a child is among the lowest levels of existence, for it is among the special properties of what cannot endure, as has been said. What they say is not merely taking a child, but His taking one, and that there be gods with Him. There is no doubt that this is not included within the bounds of possibility, let alone falling under existence. Its being among the lowest levels of existence applies only in relation to one whose nature is such.

(p-175) ﴿tusabbihu﴾ with the taa' at the top (i.e., the feminine/second form, read with ta' fawqaniyya). It is also read with the ya' below (yusabbihu). It is also read as (sabbahat), in the past tense: ﴿lahu al-samawatu al-sab'u wa'l-ardu wa man fihinna﴾ (the seven heavens, the earth, and whoever is in them) of the angels and the two weighty creatures (jinn and humankind). This is on the basis that the meaning of "tasbih" is a comprehensive one that includes what is expressed by the tongue of speech and the tongue of circumstance, by way of the broad scope of metaphor.

﴿wa in min shay'in﴾ of things, whether it be an animal, a plant, or an inanimate object.

﴿illa yusabbihu﴾ while being accompanied ﴿bi-hamdihi﴾, that is: it glorifies Him, exalted is He, by the tongue of circumstance, far above what is not befitting to His most holy Essence, from the necessary attributes of contingency and the attendant features of origination. For every existent thing, by its contingency and its origination, clearly indicates that it has a Creator who is All-Knowing, All-Powerful, All-Wise, and Necessary of existence in Himself, thereby cutting off the infinite chain.

﴿wa lakin la tafqahuna tasbihahum﴾ O polytheists, because of your neglect of the correct reflection through which this is understood. It is also read as la yufaqqahuna, in the passive form of the causative (tafil) pattern.

﴿innahu kana haliman﴾ and for this reason He did not hasten to punish you, despite your being deserving of its causes through turning away from reflection upon the clear proofs that indicate God's oneness, and your immersion in disbelief and associating partners with Him.

﴿ghafuran﴾ for whoever among you repents.

﴿And when you recite the Qur'an﴾, the one that speaks of glorifying and declaring God free of imperfection, and you call them to act upon what it contains of monotheism, rejecting polytheism, and other laws.

﴿We placed﴾ by Our power and Our will, which are based on the motives of hidden wisdoms.

﴿between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾: the relative pronoun الذين (alladhina, "those who") was preferred over the pronoun (ضمير, damir) in order to censure them by what lies within its clause (صلة, silah). The specific mention of their disbelief in the Hereafter, out of all the other things they disbelieved in, such as monotheism and the like, is to indicate that it is the greatest of what they were commanded to believe in the Qur'an, and as a preparation for what will later be reported of them regarding their denial of resurrection, their demand for it to be hastened, and similar matters.

﴿a barrier﴾ which prevents them from perceiving you as you are, in terms of prophethood, and from understanding your exalted rank. Because of this, they dared to utter the monstrous statement, which is their saying: ﴿You follow none but a man under a spell﴾. Or the barrier may be understood in light of what is reported from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with her and her father, that: "When the surah 'Tabbat' was revealed, al-'Awra' Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab, came with a stone in her hand, while the Prophet ﷺ was sitting in the mosque with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. When he saw her, he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this woman has come, and I fear she will see you.' He ﷺ said: 'She will not see me.' And he recited a Qur'an, and she stopped in front of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and did not see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." This is something that sound taste does not accept, and the noble composition does not support.

﴿hidden﴾: having a veil, as in their saying: "a flooding torrent" (سيل مفعم), or "hidden from the senses," meaning non-sensory; or hidden in itself by another barrier; or its being a barrier is hidden, since they do not realize that they do not realize.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾: *aghṭiyah* (coverings), many of them, the plural of *kinān*.

﴿Lest they understand it﴾: *an yafqahūhu* is a *maf'ūl li-ajlihi* (object of purpose; an accusative of cause or reason). The sense is "out of aversion to their understanding it," or it is an object of purpose for what the discourse implies, meaning: We prevented them from comprehending its reality and from recognizing that it is from Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And in their ears is a heaviness﴾: *ṣamamun* (deafness) and a *thiqal* (heaviness) that prevents them from hearing it as it deserves. These are figurative expressions indicating the completeness of their ignorance of the affairs of the Prophet (ﷺ), the extreme aversion of their hearts from understanding the Noble Qur'an, and the rejection of their ears toward it. They are presented as an explanation of their not understanding the eloquent tongue of speech, following the explanation of their not understanding the tongue of state (*lisān al-ḥāl*), and as a notice that this glorification is so manifest that its not being understood is conceivable only through a strong impediment that overcomes the faculties and nullifies them. They also serve as a warning that their present condition is worse than their former condition. It is not a narration of what they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is a heaviness, and between us and you there is a veil﴾. How could it not be so? Their intention in that statement is only to report what they believed, out of ignorance and disbelief, regarding the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ): that both are characterized by attributes that prevent belief and faith, such as the Qur'an being sorcery, poetry, and fables. Apply the same to the state of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is not a report that there is some matter beyond what they perceived which has placed between them and its perception a barrier from their side. There is no doubt that this meaning is hardly suited to the context.

﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾: *waḥdahu*, meaning singular, not accompanied by their gods. It is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) occupying the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative); its original form is *yaḥdū ḥaddahu*.

﴿They turn their backs﴾: that is, they fled and recoiled, ﴿in aversion﴾, or they turned away as those who recoil.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 17, verse 47:**

﴿We know best what they listen to﴾ while engaged in it, from idle talk, ridicule, and mockery of you and of the Qur'an. It is related that "two men from the clan of Banu Abd al-Dar would stand on his right side (ﷺ) and two on his left, and they would clap, whistle, and confuse him with poetry."

﴿when they listen to you﴾ is an adverbial clause of time (*zarf*, an adverb indicating time or place) governing "We know best" (*a'lam*). Its purpose is to emphasize the warning by stating that, just as this listening occurs on their part, knowledge is connected to it. This does not mean that knowledge is acquired there from anyone. The same applies to His words, exalted is He, ﴿and when they are in secret conference﴾. However, the connection is not through what the listening is directed at, but through what the secret conference is about, which is indicated by the context of the discourse. The meaning is: We know best what they listen to, of the kind that contains no good, from the matters mentioned, and what they discuss in secret among themselves. Alternatively, the first (*zarf*) modifies "they listen," and the second modifies "they confer in secret." The meaning then is: We know best what they listen to at the very time of their listening, without delay, and what they confer about at the time of their conferring. "Secret conference" (*najwa*) is in the nominative as a predicate, with an omitted governed noun (*mudaf*) understood, meaning "those who are in secret conference." Or it is the plural of *najiyy*, as *qatla* is the plural of *qatil*, meaning "those who confer in secret."

﴿when the wrongdoers say﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, an appositive that replaces the preceding term) for "when they." In it is evidence that what they confer about differs from what they listen to. The wrongdoers are placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that they are wrongdoers in this matter, transgressing the limit. That is, each of them says to the others during their secret conference:

﴿You follow﴾ either: what you follow, if following is found among you by supposition; or: what you follow of idle talk and mockery.

﴿none but a man bewitched﴾ meaning: he has been bewitched and has become insane; or a man who has *sihr*, that is, a windpipe (*ri'ah*) with which he breathes, meaning a human being like you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 48:

﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you﴾ That is: they describe you as a poet, a sorcerer, and a madman.

﴿So they have gone astray﴾ in all of that, from the method of argumentation (minhaj al-muhajjah).

﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to a criticism that anyone could accept, so they stumble about, flounder, and produce what no one doubts is false; or [they cannot find] a way to the path of truth and right guidance. In it there is a threat, and consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), of no small measure.

(p-177) ﴿And they say: "When we are bones and crumbled particles, shall we indeed be raised up in a new creation?"﴾ This is an interrogative of denial, expressing the utmost remoteness (of the matter) and rejection of resurrection after the state has come to this end, because of the incompatibility between the softness of the living and the dryness of the decayed bones; it is as if the impossibility of the matter is so evident that the addressee cannot even bring himself to speak of it. And "rufat" (crumbled particles) refers to that which has been pounded and ground to excess. Al-Farra' said: it is dust, and this is the view of Mujahid. It was also said: it is debris. And "idha" (when) is purely temporal, and this is the more apparent view. Its governing element (ʿamil) is what is indicated by His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ and not the statement itself, because what follows inna, the hamza and the lam does not govern what precedes them. The governing element is "nub'athu" (we are raised) or "nu'adu" (we are returned), and this is the object of denial. Restricting it to the mentioned time does not specify it to that time, for they deny revival after death even if the body remains in its condition; rather, it is to strengthen the denial of resurrection by directing it toward a state incompatible with it. The repetition of the hamza in their saying "a-innā" serves to emphasize the rejection, and the adornment of the sentence with "inna" and the lam serves to emphasize the denial, not to deny the emphasis, as might be suspected from the apparent wording; for the placement of the hamza before the particle is because it requires initial position, as in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ and its parallels, according to the view of the majority. Thus its meaning, according to them, is that the denial follows (the statement), not the denial of the sequence, as is well known. The basis of their denial is not that they are established as being in the state of being resurrected in actuality while in the condition of being bones and crumbled particles, as the apparent nominal sentence might suggest; rather, it is that they are in a state of readiness for that and prepared for it, and its reference is to the denial of resurrection after that state. In this there is an indication of their extreme disbelief and persistence in misguidance beyond which nothing more can be added.

﴿a new creation﴾ is in the accusative either as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) without its verb, or as a circumstantial (hal), on the basis that "khalq" (creation) is in the sense of "makhluq" (created thing).

Say: be stones or iron.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 50:

"Say" (﴿قُلْ﴾), as a reply to them, and close to what they found far-fetched.

﴿Be stones or iron.﴾

﴿Or a creation﴾ ﴿of what is greater in your breasts﴾: i.e., what is greatest in your estimation with regard to accepting life, because of the complete opposition and incompatibility between it and life. "For you are certainly going to be resurrected and returned, without doubt."

﴿So they will say: "Who will bring us back?"﴾ Despite the great distance and opposition between us and being brought back.

﴿Say﴾ to them, to affirm the truth, to remove their astonishment, and to guide them to the method of reasoning.

﴿"He who﴾ i.e., the one who will bring you back is the Mighty, Powerful One ﴿who created you﴾ brought you into existence ﴿the first time﴾ without any model to imitate or method to follow, and you were dust that had not smelled the fragrance of life. Is not He who is able to do that able to return the decayed bones to their former state? Indeed, He is capable of all things."

﴿So they will shake their heads at you﴾ i.e., they will move their heads toward you in amazement and denial, ﴿and say﴾ mockingly:

﴿"When will it be?"﴾ i.e., when will what you have mentioned of the return happen? ﴿Say﴾ to them: ﴿"It may be that it will be soon."﴾ This word "soon" is in the accusative, either as the predicate (khabar) of "yakūna" (will be), or as an adverbial (ẓarf) if "kāna" is complete (tāmmah), meaning: that it will occur in a near time.

The "an" (that) and what follows it in its clause (ḥayyiz) is either in the accusative as the predicate of "'asā" (it may be), where "'asā" is incomplete (nāqiṣah) and its subject is a pronoun referring back to what the previous statement referred to, meaning: "It may be that the resurrection will be soon," or "It may be that the resurrection occurs in a near time." Or it is in the nominative as the subject (fā'il) of "'asā," where "'asā" is complete (tāmmah), meaning: "It may be that its being soon," or "its occurrence in a near time."

﴿Yawma yad'ukum﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning "remember" (udhkurū). It may also be a substitute (badal) for qarīban, taken as an adverb of time (ẓarf). It may be a complete (tāmma) form of the verb "to be" (yakūnu) by consensus, or an incomplete (nāqiṣa) form according to those who permit the incomplete kāna to govern adverbs of time and place. It may also be governed by the implicit pronoun of the verbal noun (ḍamīr al-maṣdar al-mustakinn) in ʿasā. Or the implicit pronoun may refer to al-baʿth (the resurrection), according to those who permit the governing of the pronoun of the verbal noun, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

*"War is nothing but what you have known and tasted,
and he is not concerning it a speech of guesswork."*

Here "huwa" is the pronoun of the verbal noun, and what follows it, the prepositional phrase (al-jār), is attached to it.

﴿Fa-tastajībūna﴾ means: on the day He calls you, you will be resurrected. The verb "calling" (duʿāʾ) and "responding" (ijāba) are used figuratively for these two acts, to indicate how easily they are accomplished, and that the purpose of both is to bring you forth for reckoning. The phrase ﴿bi-ḥamdihi﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in tastajībūna, meaning: submitting to Him, praising Him for what has been done to you, and not disobeying. Or it means: praising Him, exalted is He, for His perfect power, upon witnessing its effects and beholding its decrees.

﴿Wa-tazunnūna﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with tastajībūna, meaning: you will think, when you see what you see of the awesome matters.

﴿In labittum﴾ means: how long you tarried in the graves, ﴿illā qalīlan﴾ "but a little," like the one who passed by a village, or how long you tarried in this world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 53:

﴿And say to My servants﴾, i.e., the believers, ﴿that they should say﴾ when they dispute with the polytheists ﴿that which is best﴾. i.e., the word that is best. And they should not be harsh with them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾.

﴿Indeed, Satan incites [discord] among them﴾, i.e., he corrupts and stirs up evil and contention, and incites some of them against others, so that enmity (mushaqqah), harm (mushharrah), obstruction (ma'arrah) and injury (mudarrah) occur among them. Thus that may lead to the confirmation of animosity and the continuation of corruption. So it is a justification (ta'lil) for the preceding command. It is also recited with a kasra on the zay (yanzighu): ﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been to mankind an open enemy﴾, i.e., of manifest enmity. This is a justification for what preceded, that Satan incites [discord] among them.

Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy on you, by granting you success in faith.

Or if He wills, He will punish you, by causing you to die in disbelief. This is the explanation of "that which is best," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraDh). That is, say to them this statement and what resembles it, and do not explicitly declare that they are among the people of the Fire, for that would stir them up to evil, while the outcome is something only Allah, glorified is He, knows. Perhaps He will guide them to faith.

﴿And We have not sent you over them as a guardian﴾, entrusted with their affairs, to compel them to faith. Rather, We have sent you only as a bringer of good news and a warner. So be tolerant with them, and command your companions to be tolerant, forbearing, and to abandon contention and hostility. This was before the revelation of the verse of the sword. It has also been said: this verse was revealed concerning ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, when a man insulted him, and he was commanded to pardon. It has also been said: the harm inflicted by the polytheists upon the believers became severe, so they complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed. It has also been said: the statement that is best is that they say, "May Allah guide you," and "May Allah have mercy on you."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 55:

﴿And your Lord is most knowing of those in the heavens and the earth.﴾ (p-179) And of the details of their circumstances, both apparent and hidden, by which they become worthy of being chosen and selected. So He chooses for His prophethood and His guardianship whomever He wills among those who deserve it. This is a rebuttal of them when they said: "It is far-fetched that the orphan of Abu Talib should be a prophet," and that the naked, hungry poor should be his companions rather than the great ones and the chiefs. The mention of those in the heavens is to nullify their statement: ﴿Why were the angels not sent down to us?﴾ The mention of those on the earth is to refute their statement: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾

﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ by spiritual virtues and freedom from bodily attachments, not by abundance of wealth and followers.

﴿And We gave David the Psalms﴾ is an explanation of the aspect of his being preferred, peace be upon him, for that is the giving of the Psalms, not the giving of kingship and sovereignty. In it is also an indication of the preference of the Prophet (ﷺ), for his lofty attributes and his being the Seal of the Prophets are recorded in the Psalms. And the intended meaning of "the righteous servants of Allah" in His statement, the Exalted: ﴿That the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ is the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community. The "Zabur" is mentioned sometimes with the definite article and sometimes indefinite, either because in origin it is a form ("fa'ul") in the sense of the passive participle, like "halub," or a verbal noun with that meaning, like "qawl." Or because the intended meaning is "We gave David a Zabur from among the scriptures," or "a part of the Zabur in which there is mention of him (ﷺ)." It was also read with a "damma" on the "zay," as a plural of "zabr" in the sense of "mazbur."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 56:

﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim [to be gods]﴾ besides Him, exalted is He, from among the angels, the Messiah, and 'Uzayr (Ezra).

﴿Then they have no power﴾ meaning, they are not able ﴿to remove the harm from you﴾ entirely, such as sickness, poverty, drought, and the like.

﴿Nor to transfer it﴾ i.e., nor to transfer it to others besides you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 57:

﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ i.e., those deities whom the polytheists call upon, from among those mentioned.

﴿seek﴾ they seek for themselves ﴿towards their Lord﴾ and the Owner of their affairs, ﴿the means﴾ (wasilah), i.e., nearness through obedience and worship.

﴿which of them is nearest﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the subject of "yabtaghun" (seek), and "ayyu" (which) is a relative (mawsulah). That is: they seek, [namely] the one who is nearest to Him, exalted is He, the means; so how [much less] those other than Him? Or "ibtigha'" (seeking) is taken to imply the meaning of "hirs" (eager striving), so it is as if it were said: they eagerly strive, each of them, to be nearest to Him, exalted is He, through obedience and worship. ﴿And they hope for His mercy﴾ through it ﴿and fear His punishment﴾ by abandoning it, like the custom of the rest of the servants. So where are they from removing harm, let alone divinity? ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is ever something to be feared﴾, deserving that everyone should beware of it, even the angels and the messengers, peace be upon them. This is a reason (ta'lil) for His saying, "and they fear His punishment," and its specification as the reason is because the context is one of warning against punishment, and because between them and the punishment there is a vast distance.

﴿And there is not a town﴾ is an explanation of the certainty that His punishment will befall it, with "man" (meaning "any"), so that it cannot be guarded against. This follows the explanation that it is worthy of being guarded against, and that the pillars of creation, among the angels and the prophets, peace be upon them, are wary of it. The word "in" is negative, "min" is *istighraqiyyah* (expressing totality), and "the town" means the town of disbelief: there is no town of the disbelievers ﴿but We will destroy it﴾. That is, We will utterly ruin it by causing it to sink into the earth, or by annihilating its people completely, because of the grave, destructive sins they committed that call for this. The use of the active participle, although it has the sense of the future, lacks the indication of certainty and settledness. It was said ﴿before the Day of Resurrection﴾ because destruction on that day is not specific to the disbelieving towns, nor is it by way of punishment; it is rather for the expiry of the lifespan of the world. ﴿Or punish it﴾, that is, punish its people, through *isnad majazi* (metonymic attribution), ﴿with a severe punishment﴾, not merely by killing, captivity and the like of worldly afflictions, but also by kinds of otherworldly punishment whose reality cannot be comprehended. This is what the unrestricted use of "punish," not restricted by "before the Day of Resurrection" as destruction was, makes clear. How could it be otherwise? Many of the defiant, rebellious towns have had their punishments deferred until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿That﴾ which has been mentioned of destruction and punishment ﴿was in the Book﴾, that is, the Preserved Tablet, ﴿inscribed﴾, written, with nothing left out of it but that it has been made clear in it, with its modes, its causes that necessitate it, and its appointed time. It has been said that destruction is for the righteous towns and punishment is for the wicked ones. From Muqatil: "I found in the book of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, in its interpretation: As for Mecca, the Abyssinians will ruin it; Medina will perish by hunger, Basra by drowning, Kufa by the Turks, and the mountains by thunderbolts and quakes. As for Khurasan, its destruction takes many forms," and then he mentioned it town by town.

Al-Hafiz Abu 'Amr al-Dani said in *al-Fitan* (The Book of Trials): It has been narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that al-Jazira is safe from ruin until Armenia is ruined, Armenia is safe until Egypt is ruined, Egypt is safe until Kufa is ruined, and the Great Battle (*al-Malhamah al-Kubra*) will not occur until Kufa is ruined. When the Great Battle occurs, Constantinople will be conquered at the hands of a man from the Banu Hashim. The ruin of al-Andalus will come from the direction of the Zanj, the ruin of Ifriqiya from al-Andalus, the ruin of Egypt from the cutting off of the Nile and the disagreement of armies within it, the ruin of Iraq from hunger, the ruin of Kufa from an enemy behind them who besieges them until they cannot drink a single drop from the Euphrates, the ruin of Basra from drowning, the ruin of Ayla from an enemy who besieges them by land and sea, the ruin of al-Rayy from the Daylam, the ruin of Khurasan from Tibet, the ruin of Tibet from China, the ruin of India and Yemen from locusts and the sultan, the ruin of Mecca from the Abyssinians, and the ruin of Medina from hunger.

From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The last of the towns of Islam to be ruined will be Medina." Al-'Umari has narrated it through this route.

And you are aware that generalizing "town" is supported neither by the preceding context (*al-sibaq*) nor by the subsequent context (*al-siyaq*).

And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs (ayat), meaning the signs that Quraysh proposed, such as raising the dead, turning the Safa into gold, and the like.

﴿except that the former peoples denied them﴾. This is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh, an exception from an unrestricted general term) meaning: nothing prevented Us from sending them, except the denial of the former peoples when the signs came to them as they had proposed. Their non-sending by Allah, the Exalted, was by His will, which is based on profound wisdoms and not because any preventer, whether denial or something else, restrained Him, since incapacity is impossible for Allah, the Exalted. Rather, their denial mentioned here, through its consequence of their annihilation (isti'sal) by the established divine custom (sunnah), and its implication of the denial of the others by the principle of sharing in rebelliousness and equipment, and its leading to what befell them befalling these (later) people by the principle of sharing in the crime, was incompatible with sending what they had proposed of the signs. This is because it would specify a denial that calls for annihilation, which contradicts what the pen of divine decree has written, namely the postponement of the punishments of this nation until the Hereafter, for manifest wisdoms, among which is what is supposed of the faith of some of their descendants. He expressed this incompatibility by "prevention" in the manner of metaphor (isti'arah), signalling the mutual support of the principles of sending. This is not as they claimed, that Allah did not will to support His Prophet ﷺ with miracles. This is the secret behind choosing "sending" (irsal) over "giving" (ita'), because it implies that the signs are poised to descend were it not that the hand of decree holds them back. The attribution of this prevention to the denial of the former peoples, rather than to His knowledge of what will happen from the latter peoples, is as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were refusing﴾ (8:23), in order to establish the proof against them by displaying the model, and to signal that the basis of non-response to their proposal lies only in their own conduct.

﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel﴾. This is coordinated (ma'tuf) with what the noble composition reveals, as if it were said: ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾, where We gave them the manifest signs they proposed, and they denied them; and We gave Thamud, in response to their proposal, the she-camel.

﴿Visible (mubsirah)﴾ is in the active form, meaning: a clear proof possessing sight, or insights that people perceive. Or sight is attributed to it metaphorically, as the state of one who witnesses it. Or it makes them possessors of insight, as one who causes another to see makes him seeing. It is also read in the passive form, with the mim and sad vowelled with fatha, and then it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). It is also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

﴿But they wronged themselves by it﴾, meaning they disbelieved in it while being wrongdoers. That is, they did not suffice with mere disbelief in it, but they did to it what they did of slaughtering it. Or, they wronged themselves and exposed themselves to destruction through its slaughter. Perhaps the specific mention of it is because Thamud were Arabs like them, and they have the most complete knowledge of their condition, as they witness the traces of their destruction, by coming to and turning away from it. Or because, as a living creature brought out of rock, it is the clearest proof of the truth of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Be you stones or iron﴾ (17:50).

﴿And We do not send the signs (of the proposed kind)﴾ ﴿except as a warning﴾ to those upon whom they are sent, of the destroying punishment that follows them, as a vanguard for it. Since they did not fear that, what was done to them was done. Therefore the clause has no grammatical place (mahall min al-i'rab) in that case. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "wronged", meaning: they wronged by it, and did not fear its consequence, while the state is that We do not send the signs, which are among its kind, except as a warning of the punishment that follows them, so there befell them what befell them.

﴿And [remember] when We said to you, "Indeed your Lord encompasses the people"﴾ meaning, in knowledge, as al-Imam al-Tha'labi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Nothing of their deeds is hidden from Him, whether past or future, of disbelief and denial. And [this is connected to] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾ to the end of the verse. This is a reminder of its being realized, by using as evidence what proceeded from them when some of the signs came, because all of them share in being extraordinary matters contrary to habit, sent down from Allah, glorified is He, to confirm the Prophet (ﷺ). So their denial of some of them necessitates denial of the rest, just as their denial of the others, apart from those they proposed, indicates their denial of the signs they proposed.

By "the vision" is meant what he (ﷺ) witnessed on the night of the Mi'raj of the wonders of the earth and the heaven, as is mentioned at the opening of this noble surah. The expression of that as "vision" is either because there is no difference between "ru'ya" (dream/vision) and "ru'yah" (seeing), or because it occurred at night, or because the disbelievers said, "Perhaps it was a dream." That is, "And We did not make the vision which We showed you, [shown] as a direct witnessing, even though it is a great sign, and what a true sign it is, such that no one with even a little insight would hesitate in affirming it, except as a trial by which people were tested, until some of them apostatized."

﴿And the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾ is a conjunction with "the vision." The meaning of its being cursed in it is the cursing of those who eat from it, by way of the metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi, the attributing of an action to something other than its true agent), or its being distanced from mercy, for it grows at the root of Hellfire, in the farthest place from mercy. That is: "And We did not make it except as a trial for them, since they denied it and said, 'Muhammad claims that the Hellfire burns stones, then he says that trees grow in it!'" They strayed far in that error, as they contradicted the dictates of their own intellects, for they see the ostrich swallowing embers and pieces of heated iron without harm to it, and they witness handkerchiefs made of the wool of the salamander being thrown into fire without it affecting them, and they see that in every tree there is fire. It was also read in the nominative (al-raf') by omitting the predicate, as if it were said: "And the accursed tree in the Qur'an is likewise."

﴿And We frighten them﴾ with that, and with its counterparts among the signs, for all of them serve as warnings. The choice of the present/future form (sigha al-istiqbal) indicates renewal and continuity. ﴿But it increases them only in great transgression﴾ exceeding the limit. So if We had sent the signs they proposed, they would have done with them what they did with their counterparts, and what was done to their like would be done to them. We have decided to delay the general punishment for this community until the Great Catastrophe. This is what the noble composition (al-nazm al-karim, the structure of the Qur'anic text) calls for. Most exegetes, however, have taken "encompassing" to mean encompassing by power, as a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what may afflict him from the non-fulfillment of his request for the signs they proposed to be sent down, since sending them down would not be in the interest, lest he grieve over the disbelievers' taunts, for they used to say, "If you were truly a messenger, you would have brought these miracles, as Musa and the other prophets, peace be upon them, brought."

So it is as if it were said: Remember the time when We said to you, "Indeed your Lord, Who is gentle with you, has encompassed the people. They are within the grip of His power and cannot escape His will. So He protects you from them, so do not be concerned about them, and proceed with what I commanded you of conveying the message." Do you not see that the vision which We showed you before, We made it a trial for the people, causing doubt, although it did not weaken your cause or cool your condition?

The encompassing has been interpreted as the destruction of Quraysh on the Day of Badr. The past tense is used for it although it was awaited, as indicated by His saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ and His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome and gathered to Hell﴾, and other such verses, in keeping with His, glorified is He, customary manner in His reports. The vision has also been interpreted as what he (ﷺ) saw in a dream of their places of slaughter, based on what is narrated: that when he (ﷺ) arrived at the water of Badr, he said, "By Allah, it is as if I am looking at the places where the people will fall," gesturing to the ground, "this is the place where so-and-so will fall, and this is the place where so-and-so will fall." Quraysh heard of this and mocked him. And what the Prophet (ﷺ) saw, that he would enter Mecca, and he informed his companions, so he set out toward it, but the polytheists prevented him at Hudaybiyyah in that year. The objection that what was mentioned is Medinan may be answered by saying that the revelation of their destruction could have been in Mecca, and likewise the vision.

Yet you should know that the mention of the vision, and the specification of the places of falling as actual events, [occurring] after the Hijrah, implies that the people's being tested by that occurred after the Hijrah, and that their increase in transgression was something anticipated and not yet realized at the time of the revelation of the verse. It has also been said: the vision was what he (ﷺ) saw at the battle of Badr, from the content of His saying: ﴿When Allah showed them to you in your dream as few; and had He shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾. There is no doubt that this vision, even though it occurred in Medina, was not made a trial for the people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 61:

﴿And when We said to the angels﴾ is a reminder of what Allah, exalted is He, had commanded, and of the angels' immediate compliance and obedience without hesitation, and a confirmation of the meaning of what preceded it in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord, [each] of them seeking [to be] nearer, and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾. It is understood from the state of the angels the state of others, such as Jesus and Ezra, peace be upon them both, in obedience, seeking the means of access, hoping for mercy, and fearing punishment. And from the state of Iblis is understood the state of one who opposes the truth and disobeys the command. That is: remember the time when We said to them: ﴿Prostrate yourselves before Adam﴾, as a greeting and an honouring of what he possessed of virtues that merited it. ﴿So they prostrated﴾ to him without any delay, in compliance with the command and in fulfilment of his right upon them, upon him be blessings and peace.

﴿Except Iblis﴾, who was among their company and included under the command to prostrate.

﴿He said﴾, that is, when he was rebuked by His words, may His authority be exalted: ﴿O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ and His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ and His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two hands?﴾ as was indicated in surah al-Hijr: ﴿Shall I prostrate to one whom I created from clay?﴾ — [he said] "Shall I prostrate" while I am created from the higher element, ﴿to one You created from clay﴾. The word ﴿طِينًا﴾ (ṭīnan) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naza' al-khafḍ), that is, "from clay." Or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the returning pronoun (al-rājiʿ, ﴿الرّاجِعِ﴾) to the relative pronoun, that is: You created him while he was clay. Or it is from the relative pronoun itself, that is: Shall I prostrate to him, whose origin is clay. Expressing him (ﷺ) by the relative pronoun is to give the reason for his denial through what is contained in the relative clause.

﴿He said﴾, that is, Iblis. But not immediately after his speech being related here. Rather, it was after the respite, which follows from his request for respite, which in turn follows from the command to leave the company of the Exalted Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la) under perpetual curse. The reason this is not stated explicitly is that it is sufficiently mentioned in other places. The placement of "he said" between the two statements of the accursed one indicates that the second statement is not connected to the first, and is not built upon it, but rather upon something else, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿He said: "Then what is your business?"﴾ after His Exalted saying: ﴿He said: "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the misguided?"﴾.

﴿"Tell me, is this the one You have honored above me?"﴾ The particle "al-kaf" (ال كاف, the attached "ka") is for emphasizing the address and has no place in the i'rab (grammatical case analysis). "This" is the first object, and the relative pronoun is its attribute. The second object is omitted, because the relative clause indicates it. The meaning is: "Inform me about this one whom You have honored above me by commanding me to prostrate to him, why You honored him above me." It was also said that "this" is a subject (mubtada'), from which the interrogative particle has been dropped, and the relative pronoun with its clause is its predicate. Its intent is belittlement and contempt, meaning: "Inform me, is this the one whom You have honored above me?" It was also said that the meaning of "ara'aytaka" (أرأيتك, "have you considered") is "have you pondered?", as if the speaker is alerting the addressee to bring to mind what he is about to say to him.

﴿"If You delay me"﴾ alive ﴿"until the Day of Resurrection"﴾. This is an independent statement; the "lam" is introductory to an oath, and its answer is his saying: ﴿"I will surely seize his descendants"﴾, that is: I will uproot them, from the saying of the people: "the locust stripped the earth (ihtanaka al-jaradu al-ard)" when it stripped everything upon it by eating. Or: I will lead them wherever I wish, and I will gain mastery over them with a strong mastery, from the saying of the people: "I bridled the animal (hanaktu al-dabbata) and I bridled it (ihtanaktuha)", when you put a rope around its lower jaw to lead it with. This is like His saying: ﴿"I will surely beautify for them on earth and will surely mislead them all"﴾. The fact that this aim would be achieved for him was known either by reception from the angels, peace be upon them, or by inference from their saying: ﴿"Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?"﴾, or by a guess from his own creation.

﴿"Except a few"﴾ of them, and they are the sincere (al-mukhlasun) whom God, Exalted is He, has protected.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 63:

﴿He said, "Go away."﴾ That is: proceed to your affair which you have chosen. It is a rejection of him, and a leaving of him free to pursue what his soul has embellished for him.

﴿As for whoever among them follows you, indeed Hell is your recompense, the recompense of you all.﴾ That is: the recompense of you, and the recompense of them. The addressee (al-mukhatab) was given precedence over the absent party (al-ghaib), out of regard for the right of the one who is followed (al-matbu'iyyah). ﴿A full recompense.﴾ That is: a complete recompense, from their saying: "Fir li-sahibika 'irdahu firratan," meaning: "Make it complete (waffir)." It is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing what is contained in His words ﴿indeed Hell is your recompense﴾ in the sense of "you will be recompensed" (tujazun), or it is a substitute for an implied verb, or it is a preparatory circumstantial accusative (hal muwatti'ah) for His words "mawfuran" (full).

(p-184) ﴿وَاسْتَفْزِزْ﴾ i.e., *istakhiff* (to incite, provoke to lightness and folly).

﴿مَنِ اسْتَطَعْتَ مِنْهُمْ﴾ [whoever among them you can] to incite ﴿بِصَوْتِكَ﴾ [with your voice], i.e., with your calling them to corruption, ﴿وَأَجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ i.e., shout against them, from *al-jalaba* (the clamor), which is shouting.

﴿بِخَيْلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ﴾ i.e., with your helpers and supporters, from riders and walkers, from the people of frivolity and corruption. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid and Qatada said: he has horses and foot soldiers from among the jinn and mankind. Whoever is a rider fighting in disobedience to Allah the Exalted is from the horsemen of Iblis, and whoever is a walker fighting in disobedience to Allah the Exalted is from the foot soldiers of Iblis. *Al-khayl* means the horsemen. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O horsemen of Allah, mount!" *Al-rajl* is a collective noun for *al-rajil* (walker), like *al-sahb* and *al-rakb*. It has been recited with a kasra on the *jim* (*rijal*), which is the reading of Hafs, taking it as *fi'il* in the sense of *fa'il*, like *ta'ib* and *ta'ib*; and with a damma, like *hadath* and *hudut*, *nadis* and *nudus*, and their likes; meaning: gather your walkers to match the horsemen. It has also been recited *rijalika* and *warijalika*. It is possible that his inciting is by his voice, and his summoning against them is with his horsemen and foot soldiers, as a representation of his dominance over those whom he misleads. He is like a fierce warrior who falls upon a people, shouts at them with a voice that disturbs them from their places and unsettles them from their positions, and summons against them his army of horsemen and foot soldiers until he uproots them.

﴿وَشَارِكْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْوَالِ﴾ by urging them to acquire and gather them from what is forbidden, and to dispose of them in ways that are not proper.

﴿وَالْأَوْلَادِ﴾ by urging them to reach them through forbidden means, and by association (*ishrak*), such as naming them ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, and by misguidance through leading them to deviant religions, despicable trades, and vile deeds.

﴿وَعِدْهُمْ﴾ with false promises, such as the intercession of the gods, relying on the honor of forefathers, and delaying repentance by prolonging hope. ﴿وَمَا يَعِدُهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ إِلَّا غُرُورًا﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) to explain the nature of his promises. The shift to the third person (*iltifat*) strengthens the sense of the parenthetical clause, together with what it contains of turning the speech away from addressing him, explaining his nature to people, and indicating the causal link between his being a devil (*shaytana*) and his deceiving (*ghurur*), which is making error appear attractive by what makes it seem to be right.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 65:

﴿Indeed, My servants﴾ The idafa (annexation, i.e. the construction linking "servants" to "My") is for honour (ridicule-free dignification), and they are the sincere ones (al-mukhlasun). In this it is implied that whoever follows him (Satan) is not among them. And the idafa indicates the establishment of the ruling in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You have no authority over them﴾, meaning: no dominion and no power over leading them astray, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾.

﴿And your Lord is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs (wakil)﴾ for them: they rely upon Him and seek His help in being delivered from your misguidance. The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates absolute ownership and comprehensive disposal, together with the annexation to the pronoun of Iblis, serves to signal the manner of His sufficiency for them, namely the stripping away of his power to lead them astray.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 66:

﴿Your Lord is He who drives the ships for you through the sea﴾ — a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). Al-izja' (driving, propelling) means al-sawq (driving on). "Hālan ba'da hāl" (a state after a state) means: He is the Powerful, the Wise, who drives the ships for your benefits and makes them run in the sea.

﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾ — of His provision, which is a bounty from Him, or of the profit which He grants. The "min" (from) is either superfluous (mazīdah) or partitive (tab'īḍiyyah). This is a reminder of some of the blessings which are evidences of tawhid (Oneness of God), and a preparation for the mention of their affirmation of tawhid "when harm touches them" (p-185), completing what came earlier in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so they have no power﴾ ... the verse.

﴿Indeed He is ever, toward you﴾ — eternally and everlastingly — ﴿Merciful﴾, in that He has prepared for you what you need, and made easy for you what would be difficult from its beginnings. This is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) containing a reason for what preceded concerning the driving of ships for the seeking of bounty. The form "Merciful" (raḥīm) indicates that the intended mercy is worldly mercy: the immediate blessing, which is divided into the great and the small.

﴿When harm touches you at sea﴾: the fear of drowning in it.

﴿Those whom you call upon vanish﴾: that is, what you used to call upon besides God, of the angels, or the Messiah, or others, departs from your thoughts.

﴿except Him﴾: alone, without any of them occurring to your minds, and you call upon Him to remove it, whether independently or in association. Or: all whom you call upon go astray from helping you and rescuing you, and none is able to do that except God, by way of the disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati').

﴿Then when He has delivered you﴾ from drowning, and brought you ﴿to land, you turn away﴾ from monotheism (tawhid), or you exceed in ingratitude for the blessing.

﴿And man is ever ungrateful﴾: this is an explanation of the turning away mentioned before.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 68:

﴿Do you then feel secure﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle, here expressing disapproval) and the fa' (conjunction linking to an implied clause) are used here. Its implied sense is: "Have you been saved, and so you feel secure?"

﴿that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you﴾ which is your place of safety; that is, He will overturn it while you are in it, or because of your being in it. The mention of "side" (janib) alerts to the equality of all sides and directions with respect to His power, His dominion, and His authority. It has also been read with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama), i.e., "We will cause to swallow."

﴿or send against you﴾ a storm from above you. It has also been read with the nun (i.e., "We will send").

﴿a violent wind (hasiban)﴾ a wind that pelts with pebbles, ﴿then you will not find for yourselves any guardian (wakil)﴾ who will protect you from that, or turn it away from you, for there is no one who can repel His overpowering command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 69:

﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you into it⁠—⁠﴾ into the sea. The word fi (in) has been preferred over ila (to), which indicates mere arrival, in order to signify their settling within it. ﴿another time⁠﴾. The attribution of the return to Him, the Exalted, is made even though returning to it is by their own choice, in view of His creating the motives that compel them to it. In this there is an allusion to the utmost intensity of the terror, of which there is no strength in the first instance, such that, were it not for the return, they would not have returned.

﴿then send against you﴾ while you are in the sea. It is also read with the nun (we send).

﴿a violent wind﴾ which is one that does not pass by anything without breaking it and reducing it to crumbled dust; or one that has a qasif, which is a strong sound, as if it were shattering, i.e., breaking apart.

﴿and drown you﴾ after breaking your ship, as the expression "qasf" indicates. It is also read with the nun, and with the ta' (you are drowned), as attributed to the pronoun of the wind.

﴿for your disbelief﴾ because of your associating partners, or your ingratitude for the blessing of deliverance. ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves any avenger against Us for it⁠—⁠﴾ i.e., one who pursues us, demanding what we have done in order to take revenge, and seeking redress for the vengeance on our behalf, like His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾.

(p-186) ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾, all of them, with a comprehensive honor encompassing the righteous and the wicked among them. That is: We honored them with the (upright) form and stature, with dominion over what is on the earth and enjoyment of it, with the ability to practice crafts, and other things that expression cannot fully encompass. Among its components is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, mentioned: that every animal takes its food with its mouth, except the human being, who lifts it to his mouth with his hand. As for what has been said, that the monkey shares this (trait) with him, it is based on not distinguishing between the hand and the foot, for it takes (food) with its foot, the foot with which it treads on filth, not with its hand.

﴿And We carried them on the land and the sea﴾, on beasts and ships, from "hamaltuhu" (I carried him), when you provide him with something to ride; and there is nothing among created beings that is like this. It has also been said: We carried them in them (the ships), in that We did not cause the earth to swallow them up nor drown them in water. You know that the first (meaning) is more suitable to the (theme of) honor, since all animals are like this.

﴿And We provided for them of the good things﴾, that is, kinds of blessings and varieties of pleasurable things, of what is obtained through their own labor and through other than their labor.

﴿And We preferred them﴾ in knowledge and perception, by what We placed in them of the perceptive faculties by which truth is distinguished from falsehood, and the good from the ugly.

﴿Above many of those We created﴾, namely all except the angels, peace be upon them, ﴿with a great preference﴾. It is therefore incumbent upon them to be thankful for these blessings, not to deny them, to employ their faculties in acquiring correct beliefs, and to reject the polytheism they are upon, which no one with even a little discernment accepts, let alone one who has been preferred over all besides the exalted assembly, who are pure intellects, since the genus of angels was excepted from this preference because their knowledge is permanent and free of error and defect. This does not indicate their superiority in the disputed sense, for what is intended here is the explanation of a preference in a matter shared by all individuals of mankind, the righteous and the wicked alike, and that preference cannot be the excellence in the magnitude of rank and the increase in nearness to Allah, the Exalted. If it is said: "What need is there to specify what the preference consists in, after clarifying who the preferred ones are, since excepting the angels, peace be upon them, from the preference of all individuals of mankind over them does not entail excepting them from the preference of some individuals of mankind over them?" We say: it is absolutely necessary to specify it, for among the wicked individuals of mankind there is no one who excels any created being in what is the matter in dispute at all; rather they are lower than every base thing, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are like cattle; rather, they are further astray﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of beasts in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾.

﴿On the Day We shall call﴾ is in the accusative as an object (*maf'ūliyya*, the direct object) governed by an implied verb, *udhkur* ("remember"), or it is an adverbial of time (*ẓarf*) governed by what is indicated by His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. It has also been read as ﴿yad'ū﴾ with the *yā'* (third-person masculine) both in the active and the passive voice. The word ﴿yad'ū﴾ has the *alif* changed to a *wāw*, according to the dialect of those who say *if'aw* for *if'ā* ("a snake"). It has also been permitted that the *wāw* is the sign of the plural, as in His words, ﴿and they conceal the secret counsel﴾, or that its pronoun refers to ﴿kulla﴾ ("every"), which is then a substitute (*badal*) for it. The *nūn* is omitted because of the little concern for it, since it is only the sign of the nominative. It may also be satisfied by its being presumed, as in *yud'ā*. ﴿Every people﴾ are the children of Adam, ﴿those whom﴾ (p-187) We favoured in the world with what We favoured them with of honour and preference. This is the beginning of an explanation of the variation in their states in the Hereafter according to their states and their deeds in the world.

﴿With their imam﴾ means: with those whom they followed, be it a prophet, or a leader in religion, or a book, or a religion. It has been said: with the book of their deeds which they had sent forward. Then it will be said: "O companions of the book of good! O companions of the book of evil!" Or: "O people of such-and-such a religion! O people of such-and-such a book!" It has also been said that *imam* is the plural of *umm* ("mother"), like *khuff* and *khifāf*. The wisdom in calling them by their mothers is the honouring of Jesus, peace be upon him, the exalting of al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the covering of the children of fornication.
