﴿Whoever is given﴾ on that day from among those who are called ﴿his book﴾, the record of his deeds, ﴿in his right hand﴾: to show the importance of the book that is given and to honour its owner, and to give him good news from the outset of what is within its pages. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to ﴿whoever﴾ in view of its meaning, to indicate that they are a party gathered upon a noble state, or as a notice that their reading of their books will be in a gathered manner and not individually, as in the case of the giving. The distance indicated by the demonstrative serves to signal the elevation of their ranks, i.e., those specially favoured with that honour which the aforementioned giving indicates.

﴿They will read their book﴾ which was given to them in the clear manner, in exultation at the good deeds inscribed in it, which entail all kinds of honours.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ means: they will not be diminished from the rewards of their deeds recorded in their books, but rather they will be given them multiplied.

﴿A fatīl﴾ means: the measure of a fatīl, which is the thin membrane in the split of a date-stone, or the least thing, since the *fatīl* is a proverb for smallness and insignificance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 72:

﴿And whoever is﴾ among those summoned who were mentioned.

﴿In this﴾ world, in which were done to them various kinds of honouring and favouring, ﴿blind﴾, lacking insight, unable to be guided to his right course, and not recognising the blessing of honour and favour that We bestowed upon him, let alone giving thanks for it and fulfilling its rights. He does not make use of the intellects and faculties with which We endowed him for that for which they were created, namely the true sciences and knowledge.

﴿Then he, in the Hereafter﴾, which was referred to as "a day We shall summon."

﴿Blind﴾ likewise, that is, he is not guided to what would save him, nor does he attain what would benefit him, because the first blindness necessitates the second. It has been permitted that the second be in the sense of comparison, on the basis that his blindness in the Hereafter is more severe than his blindness in this world. For this reason Abu 'Amr read the first ﴿a'mā﴾ with imalah and the second emphatically (with tafkhim).

﴿And more astray in way﴾, that is: than the blind man in this world, due to the cessation of the possible capacity and the complete disabling of the faculties. This is precisely the one who is given his book in his left hand, as indicated by the state of the opposing group mentioned before him. Perhaps the shift away from mentioning him under that designation, although it is what the excellence of the contrast would call for, as is the case in Surat al-Haqqah and Surat al-Inshiqaq, is to signal the reason that necessitates it, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿But if he is among the deniers, the astray﴾, after His words: ﴿But if he is among the companions of the right﴾. It also alludes to the cause of the state of the first group: one side mentions the effect, and the other the cause, and each side, by what is mentioned, indicates what is omitted on the other, relying on the testimony of reason, as in His words, mighty and exalted: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He intends for you good, there is none to repel His bounty﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 73:

﴿And indeed they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ It was revealed concerning Thaqif, when they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We will not enter into your affair until you give us privileges through which we may boast over the Arabs: we shall not be made to pay the tithe (ushr) or be mustered (for jihad), we shall not bow in our prayer (lit. we shall not be made to bend in our prayer), all interest owed to us shall be ours, and all interest owed by us shall be waived for us, you shall allow us to enjoy al-Lat for a year, and you shall make our valley, Wajj, sacred as you made Mecca sacred. Then when the Arabs ask, 'Why did you do this?', say: 'God commanded me to do so.'" It was also said that it was revealed concerning Quraysh, when they said: "Make for us a sign of punishment into a sign of mercy, and a sign of mercy into a sign of punishment," or they said: "We will not allow you to touch the Black Stone until you pay homage to our gods." So "in" (إنْ) is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy form (muthaqqala), the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), which is its subject, is omitted, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqa) between it and the negating "in" (إنْ النافية). That is: the matter is that they nearly tempted you, i.e., they deceived you, being tempters.

﴿from that which We revealed to you﴾ of Our commands, Our prohibitions, Our promise and Our warning.

﴿so that you would fabricate against Us other than it﴾ so that you would invent against Us something other than what We revealed to you, of what Thaqif or Quraysh proposed, as is related.

﴿And then they would have taken you as a close friend﴾ That is: if you had followed their desires, you would have been a friend to them, and you would have left My guardianship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 74:

﴿And had We not made you firm⁠﴾ upon what you were upon of the truth, by Our protection (ʿiṣma) of you.

﴿You were almost inclining toward them a little﴾ with the inclination (rukūn) which is the least degree of leaning. That is: had it not been for Our making you firm, you would have come close to inclining toward them a little, a slight degree of slight inclination, because of the strength of their deceptions and the intensity of their scheming. But the protection (ʿiṣma) overtook you, so We prevented you from coming close even to the lowest levels of inclining toward them, let alone the inclination itself. This is explicit that he (ﷺ) did not intend to comply with them despite the strength of the call to it, and it is evidence that protection (ʿiṣma) is by the granting of success (tawfīq) and care of God, the Exalted.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 75:

﴿Then﴾ had you come close to inclining toward them even slightly, ﴿We would have made you taste double in life and double in death﴾, that is: the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, double what is inflicted in both abodes upon anyone other than you for the same act; for the error of a great person is great. The original wording was "a double punishment in life and a double punishment in death," meaning "multiplied." Then the qualified noun (the punishment) was omitted and its adjective (double) was put in its place, and then it was made an idafah (construct phrase) to what it describes. It has also been said: "ḍi'f" (double) is among the names of punishment. It has also been said that what is meant by "double in life" is the punishment of the Hereafter, and by "double in death" is the punishment of the grave.

﴿Then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾, who would ward off the punishment from you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 76:

﴿And indeed they were about to﴾ The discourse here is as it was in the first part, meaning: the people of Makkah were about to ﴿provoke you﴾, that is, to drive you out with their enmity and their deceit, ﴿from the land﴾, that is, the land in which you are, which is the land of Makkah.

﴿to expel you from it. And then they would not remain﴾ With the nominative (ḍamm) ending, in conjunction with the predicate of kāda (kāna's sister: "to be about to"), and it is read: (lā yalbathū) with the accusative (naṣb) by making idhan (then, in that case) operative, on the basis that the clause is conjoined to the clause "And indeed they were about to provoke you."

﴿after you﴾ That is, after you. He said:

*The dwellings were emptied of them after them, so it was as if the combers had spread out a mat between them.* (This is a line of poetry, cited as is.)

That is: even if you had gone out, they would not remain after your going out. It is also read: (khalfaka), "behind you."

﴿except for a little﴾ Except for a little time. This is indeed what happened, for they were destroyed at Badr after his emigration (ﷺ). It is said: the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, when they envied the Prophet's (ﷺ) station in Madinah, and said: "Syria is the station of the prophets (peace be upon them). So if you are a prophet, then go there, until we believe in you." This came into the Prophet's (ﷺ) heart, so he set out one stage, then the verse was revealed, and he returned. Then the Banu Qurayzah among them were killed, and the Banu al-Nadir were expelled a short time later.

Surah 17, verse 77: Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim)

﴿Sunnata man qad arsalna qablaka min rusulina﴾ (a practice concerning those之 whom We sent before you of Our messengers). It is in the accusative as an absolute object (al-masdariyya), meaning: God Most High has established a practice (sunna), namely that He destroys every nation that expels its messenger from among them. Thus the sunna belongs to God Most High, and its attribution to the messengers is because it was established on their account, as indicated by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And you will not find any alteration in Our practice﴾, i.e., any change.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 78:

﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ at its decline (zawal), as the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated when he said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me at the decline of the sun, when it had passed its zenith, and led me in the noon prayer." Its derivation is from dalk (rubbing), because whoever looks at the sun at that time rubs his eye. It has also been said that it refers to its setting, from "dalakat al-shams," meaning the sun set. It has also been said that the root meaning of dulook is inclination (mayl), which encompasses both meanings. The lam here marks a time limit, like it in your saying: "for three nights gone by" (li-thalathin khalawna).

﴿until the darkness of the night﴾ until the gathering of its darkness, which is the time of the night prayer (al-'isha'). The intended meaning is not that one should pray continuously between the two times, but that each prayer be performed at its appointed time, which was determined by the explanation of Jibril (peace be upon him), just as the number of units (rak'at) of each prayer was entrusted to the explanation of the Prophet (ﷺ). Perhaps the mention of only the beginning and end of the prayer times without separating them is because a person between these times is awake, so some of them are connected to one another. By contrast, at the start of the night prayer's time and the dawn prayer, a person is occupied with sleep between them, so one is cut off from the other. For this reason, the time of the dawn prayer was separated from the rest of the times. It has also been said that the intended prayer is the sunset prayer (maghrib). The aforementioned limits explain its beginning and end. Scholars have cited this verse as evidence that its time extends until the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and the recitation of the dawn﴾, meaning the dawn prayer, is in the accusative as a conjunction with the object of "establish" (aqim), or as an incitement (ighra'), as al-Zajjaj said. It is called "recitation" because recitation is its pillar (rukn), just as it is called bowing (ruku') and prostration (sujud). Some have used this to argue that recitation is a pillar, but it does not indicate that, since the basis of the ruling may be that recitation in it is recommended. Yes, if it were interpreted as recitation in the dawn prayer, the command to establish it would indicate obligation in it explicitly, and in the other prayers by implication.

﴿Indeed, the recitation of the dawn﴾ The apparent noun is used in place of a pronoun to show greater emphasis on it.

﴿is witnessed﴾ It is witnessed by the angels of the night and the angels of the day. Or the signs of power in the change of light to darkness and of waking from sleep, which is the brother of death. Or many worshippers witness it. Or it is due that a great multitude should witness it. So the verse, on the interpretation of dulook as decline, includes the five prayers, and on the interpretation of it as setting, it covers all except noon and afternoon.

﴿وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ It has been said that it is in the accusative as an exhortation (al-ighra'), meaning: "Persist in part of the night." It has also been said that the object of exhortation cannot be a particle, and that the fact that its meaning is partitive (al-tab'id) is of no use, because the "wa" (and) with "ma" (in "wa-ma") is not a noun by consensus (ijma'), even if it has the meaning of an explicit noun. Rather, it is in the accusative of time (al-zarfiyyah), governed by an implied verb, meaning: "Stand (in prayer) during part of the night." ﴿فَتَهَجَّدْ بِهِ﴾ means: remove and cast off sleep (al-hujud), that is, slumber. The verbal form (sigha al-tafa''ul) comes for removal, as in "taharraja" (he removed sin), "tahannatha" (he removed wrongdoing) and "ta'atthama" (he removed sin), and similar forms. The pronoun in "bihi" (with it) refers to the Qur'an as such, so that its attachment is not restricted to the dawn; or it refers to the part understood from His words, "and during part of the night", meaning: pray during that part, with the "ba'" (with) meaning "fi" (in). It has also been said that it is governed by "yatahajjad" (he prays at night), meaning: pray with the Qur'an during part of the night, in the manner of ﴿وَإيّايَ فارْهَبُونِ﴾ (and it is Me alone you should fear).

﴿نافِلَةً لَكَ﴾ an additional obligation over and above the five obligatory prayers, specific to you alone and not to the community. Perhaps this is the reason it is mentioned after the dawn prayer, although its time precedes it. Or it is a voluntary act (ta-tawwu'), but not because it is an addition to the obligations, rather because it is an addition for him, peace be upon him, in ranks, as Mujahid and al-Suddi said. For he, peace be upon him, has been forgiven his earlier and later sins, so his voluntary worship is an addition to his ranks. This differs from the rest of the community, whose voluntary worship is for the expiation of their sins and the making up of deficiencies in their obligatory acts. Its accusative case is either as a verbal noun (masdariyyah), with the implied verb "tanaffal" (perform a supererogatory act), or by making "tahajjad" have the same meaning, or by making "nafilah" mean "tahajjudan" (night prayer), since that is an additional act of worship. Or it is in the circumstantial accusative (al-hal) from the pronoun referring to the Qur'an, meaning: while it is a supererogatory prayer. Or it is the direct object of "tahajjad" when it is taken to mean "pray", and the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the part, meaning: pray during that part as a supererogatory prayer for you.

﴿عَسى أنْ يَبْعَثَكَ رَبُّكَ﴾ "It may be that your Lord will raise you," who will bring you to your perfection fitting for you after the greater death, just as you were raised from sleep, which is the lesser death, through prayer and worship.

﴿مَقامًا﴾ is in the accusative of place/time (al-zarfiyyah), with the implied verb "fa-yuqimuka" (so He will establish you), or by including in "al-ba'th" (raising) the meaning of "al-iqamah" (establishing), since the governing verb of such an adverb must be a verb carrying the meaning of remaining. It may also be a circumstantial accusative, with an implied noun, meaning: He will raise you possessing a station.

﴿مَحْمُودًا﴾ praised by you and by all people. In this there is a lessening of the hardship of standing in prayer at night. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'The praised station is the station in which I will intercede for my community.'" And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: a station in which the first and the last will praise you, and in which you will overlook all creation, you will be asked and you will be given, you will intercede and your intercession will be accepted; no one will be except under your banner. And from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him: "People will be gathered in one plain, and no soul will speak in it. The first to be called will be Muhammad ﷺ, and he will say: 'At Your service, and at Your pleasure. The evil is not attributed to You. The one guided is he whom You have guided. Your servant is before You. By You and to You, there is no refuge nor escape except to You. You are blessed and exalted. Glory be to You, Lord of the House.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 80:

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter"﴾ i.e., the grave.

﴿with a sincere entrance﴾ i.e., an entrance that is pleasing.

﴿And cause me to exit﴾ i.e., from it, at the resurrection (al-ba'th).

﴿with a sincere exit﴾ i.e., an exit that is pleasing, met with honour. This is a teaching of supplication with what He promised him of resurrection, coupled with the well-known abode (al-iqamah al-ma'hudah) above which there is no honour. It was also said: the intended meaning is entering Medina and exiting Mecca, and the reversal of the order of existence is because entering is the goal. It was also said: his (ﷺ) entering Mecca victorious over it, and his exiting from it safe from the polytheists. It was also said: his entering the cave and his exiting from it safe. It was also said: his entering into what he bore of the burdens of the message, and his exiting from it having fulfilled its right. It was also said: his entering into everything that he is involved in, of place or matter, and his exiting from it.

It was read as (مَدْخَلَ) and (مَخْرَجَ) with a fatha, meaning: "Cause me to enter so that I may enter an entering, and cause me to exit so that I may exit an exiting," like his saying:

"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth only the scant or the scraped."

i.e., it left, so nothing remained.

﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority, a helping one﴾ — a proof that supports me against those who oppose me, or a sovereignty and might that supports Islam, making it prevail over disbelief. His (ﷺ) supplication was answered by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah protects you from the people﴾; "Verily, the party of Allah, they are the victorious"; ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾; ﴿He will surely make them successors in the land﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 81:

﴿And say: The truth has come﴾, i.e., Islam and the firm, established revelation.

﴿And falsehood has vanished﴾, i.e., it went away and perished: polytheism (shirk) and disbelief (kufr), and the enticements of Satan. It is from zahaqa ruhuhu (his soul departed), when it came out.

﴿Indeed, falsehood﴾, whatever it may be, ﴿is ever bound to vanish﴾, i.e., its nature is to be dissipated and unstable. (p-191) This is a noble promise of the answering of the supplication for the victorious authority that he was taught. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "He (ﷺ) entered Makkah on the day of the Conquest, and around the House were three hundred and sixty idols. He began to poke at the eye of each one of them with a staff that was in his hand, saying: 'The truth has come and falsehood has vanished,' and it would fall on its face until he had cast down all of them. There remained the idol of Khuza'ah above the Ka'bah, and it was of brass. He said: 'O Ali, throw it down,' so he climbed up and threw it down and broke it."

And We send down of the Qur'an, (it is) also read as nunzilu, from inzal (causing to descend).

﴿That which is a healing﴾ for what is in the breasts, from the diseases of doubt and the sicknesses of misconceptions.

﴿And a mercy for the believers﴾ who act upon it and know what is in its contents, that is, what is in the straightening of their religion and the reforming of their souls, like the healing medicine for the sick. The "min" (in "min al-Qur'an") is explanatory (bayaniyya, indicating what the thing is), placed before what it explains out of concern for it, since all of the Qur'an is of this kind. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does not seek healing through the Qur'an, may God not heal him." Or the "min" is partitive (tab'idiyya), but not in the sense that some part of it is not of this kind. Rather, the meaning is that We send down from it, on each occasion, what wisdom calls for its descent at that time, so that it falls, for those to whom it descends, because it accords with their circumstances that call for its descent, in the position of the healing medicine that happens to meet the need, not because it is from the sick who need it, according to the situation, without any change in order. So every part of it is characterized by healing, but not at all times, only at the time of its descent. The realization of partitiveness, taking healing in the physical sense, as in al-Fatiha and the verses of healing, is not supported by His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾, that is, the whole Qur'an increases, or each part of it increases, the disbelievers who deny it and who place things other than in their proper places, despite its being in itself a healing from diseases, except in loss, that is, destruction, because of their disbelief and denial, not a decrease, as has been said. For the disease of disbelief and error that they have is worthy of being expressed by destruction, not by a decrease, which would indicate that some beginnings of sicknesses have occurred in them, and by their increase in degrees of destruction, insofar as whenever they renew disbelief and denial of the verses revealed gradually, they increase in destruction thereby. In this there is an allusion that what the believers have of doubts and suspicions that befall them in the course of guidance and seeking right direction is in the position of illnesses, and what the disbelievers have of ignorance and obstinacy is in the position of death and destruction. The ascription of the mentioned increase to the Qur'an, although it is they who increase in it through their evil conduct, is on account of considering it as the cause of that, and in it there is a marvelling at its matter, in that it is the pivot of both healing and destruction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 83:

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾ with health and blessing.

﴿He turns away﴾ from remembering Us, let alone fulfilling what is required by gratitude, ﴿and turns aside﴾ far from obeying Us.

﴿With his side﴾: al-na'y bil-janib (turning aside with the side) means that one twists one's flank away from a thing and turns the broadside of one's face from it. Thus it is an emphasis of "turns away," or it is an expression for arrogance, since this is among the habits of the arrogant.

﴿And when evil touches him﴾ in the form of poverty, sickness, or any of the calamities. The attribution of touching to evil after the attribution of bestowal to the Divine Name indicates that good is intended for its own sake, whereas evil is not so intended.

﴿He was despairing﴾: exceedingly despairing of Our mercy. This is a description of the species with regard to some of its individuals who are characterised by this trait, and it is not contradicted by His words, exalted is He: ﴿and when evil touches him, he is one of abundant supplication﴾, and similar verses, for that is the condition of some others among them. It has also been said that what is meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. It is read as (nā larbaʾin / nā'in) either by metathesis, as one says rā'in for ra'ā, or because it means nahada (rose up).

(p-192) ﴿Say: "Each one acts according to his own manner (shakilah)"﴾. That is: each one of you, and each of those who oppose you, ﴿acts according to his own manner (shakilah)﴾, meaning his way that is suited to his state in guidance and misguidance. Or (shakilah means) the essence of his soul and his states that follow the temperament of his body.

﴿Your Lord is best aware of who is best guided in the way (sabil)﴾. That is: who has the straightest path and the clearest method. The word shakilah has been explained as nature (tab'), habit (adah), and religion (din).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 85:

﴿And they ask you about the soul.﴾ The apparent meaning is that the question concerned the reality of the soul (al-ruh), which is the governing principle of the human body and the source of its life. It is related that the Jews said to the Quraysh: "Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the soul. If he answers all of them or remains silent, he is not a prophet; but if he answers some and remains silent about others, then he is a prophet." So he (ﷺ) explained to them the two stories and left the matter of the soul undetermined, and it is undetermined in the Torah as well.

﴿Say: The soul is﴾ (the word is) brought forward in the position of an explicit noun rather than a pronoun, to show the complete care given to its matter, ﴿from the command of my Lord.﴾ The word "min" (from) is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and "amr" (command) means "matter" or "affair." The idafah (genitive construction) indicates specialization in knowledge, not in origination, since all things share in that; and in it there is an honouring of the annexed noun that is not hidden, just as in the second idafah there is an honouring of the noun to which it is annexed. That is, it is of the kind of hidden secrets which God the Exalted has reserved for knowledge of Himself, and which the minds of mankind scarcely approach.

﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little.﴾ This cannot be taken as referring to matters of this kind. It is related that when he (ﷺ) said this to them, they said: "We are specially addressed by this speech." He (ﷺ) said: "Rather, we and you." They said: "How wondrous is your affair: one moment you say, ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good,﴾ and another moment you say this." So there was revealed, ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens...﴾ — to the end of the verse. They only said this because of the feebleness of their intellects, for human wisdom is to know of good what human capacity can contain, indeed what livelihood and the afterlife depend upon; and that is relative to the infinity of His knowledge, glorified is He. It is a little, by which much good is attained in itself, or relative to man; or it is of the originated things that come into being purely through the command of creation, without being obtained from a material or generated from a root, like the members of the body, so that it could be defined through some of its principles. Its implication is that it is of the world of command, not of the world of creation. This is not of the kind of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ For that is an expression of the swiftness of creation, whether the created thing is of the world of command or of the world of creation. In it is an alert that it is among what the circle of human perception does not encompass in its reality; what is possible is only this general measure, falling under what is excepted by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾, that is, only a little knowledge which you acquire through the paths of the senses, for the conceiving of theoretical knowledge is only from the perception of particulars. Hence it is said: "Whoever loses a sense has lost a branch of knowledge." Perhaps most things are not perceived by the senses, nor is any of their states, upon which the knowledge of its essence depends. As for interpreting what was mentioned as concerning the question of its eternity or its createdness, and making the answer an information about its createdness, that is: it exists by His creation and is originated by His bringing into being through the command of creation, that is not suitable to the state of the questioners, and the mention of explaining their small knowledge does not support it; for what they asked about is among what their knowledge at that time could cover, and it has been informed about. It was also said: the intended meaning of the soul is a great spiritual creation, greater than the angel; it was said: it is Jibril, peace be upon him; it was said: it is the Qur'an. The meaning of "from the command of my Lord" is from His revelation and His speech, not from the speech of men.

(p-193) ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾ from the Qur'an, which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and a wellspring of the sciences that you have been given. We made you firm upon it when they almost tempted you away from it, and had it not been for it, you would almost have inclined toward them, a little. The expression "that which" (al-ladhi) is used in the relative form to magnify its status, to describe it at the outset by what is within the relative clause (silah), to inform of its condition from the very beginning, and to indicate that it is not of the kind of the speech of created beings. The "lam" (al-lam, the lam of oath) is a preparatory particle (muwatta'ah) for the oath, and "la-nadhhabanna" (we would surely take away) is its answer, which stands in place of the answer of the conditional clause. It is for this reason that the object of the will (mashi'ah) has been omitted as fine usage. What is meant by "taking it away" is its erasure from the codices (masahif) and from the hearts (sudur), and this is more emphatic than "idhhab" (removal).

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the first thing you lose of your religion is trustworthiness, and the last thing you lose is prayer; and there will be people who pray while having no religion; and this Qur'an, you will wake up one day and there will be nothing of it among you. A man said: "How can that be, when we have fixed it in our hearts and fixed it in our codices, teaching it to our sons, and our sons teach it to their sons?" He said: "It will pass over it by night, so that in the morning people will be empty of it; the codices will be lifted up, and what is in the hearts will be removed."

﴿Then you will not find for yourself against Us any ally in respect of it﴾, i.e., the Qur'an.

﴿a guardian (wakil)﴾: one who would take on the task of demanding its return to Us, preserved in writing and protected.

"Except as a mercy from your Lord." For if it reaches you, perhaps it will restore it to you. It is also permissible for the exception (*istithna'*) to be disjunctive (*munqati'*, not of the same kind as what precedes it), with the meaning: "but rather, a mercy from your Lord has left it [the Qur'an] unremoved from you." This is a favor by preserving it after the favor of sending it down, an encouragement to guard its rights by fulfilling them, and a warning against failing to appreciate its great worth and neglecting to give thanks for it. It is the most sublime and greatest of blessings.

"Indeed, His favor upon you has been great." Such as your being sent as a messenger, the sending down of the Book upon you, its preservation in your keeping, and other things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 88:

﴿Say﴾ to those who do not recognize the sublime rank of the Revelation and do not grasp the majesty of its exalted station, but rather claim that it is the speech of men.

﴿Even if mankind and the jinn gathered﴾, i.e., agreed together,

﴿to produce the like of this Qur'an﴾, described with those sublime qualities in eloquence, beauty of arrangement, and perfection of meaning that the intellects cannot grasp. The mention of the two categories (al-thaqalan, mankind and jinn) specifically is because the one who denies that it is from Allah the Exalted is from among them and not from others, not because the others are capable of opposing it.

﴿They will not produce its like﴾. The explicit noun was preferred over a pronoun referring back to the mentioned "like," to guard against the assumption that it has a specific counterpart, and to announce that the intended meaning is the negation of producing any like at all: that is, they will not bring a speech comparable to it in the wondrous qualities mentioned. Among them are the Arab al-'Aribah (the pure Arabs), masters of eloquence and clarity. This is the answer to the oath which the preceding lam (al-lam al-muwatti'ah, the introductory lam) indicates, and it takes the place of the answer of the conditional. Without that lam, it would have been an answer to the conditional without jussive, since the condition is in the past tense, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

؎ And if a close friend comes to him on the day of request, he says: "My wealth is not absent, nor is it forbidden."

Since the intended meaning of gathering together to produce the like of the Qur'an is absolute agreement upon that, whether each one of them undertakes the challenge individually or the whole group together by compiling a single speech through successive ideas and mutual support of viewpoints, it was said: ﴿and even if some of them were helpers of others﴾ (p-194), i.e., in realizing what they aim at of producing its like. This is a conjunction with an implied antecedent, i.e., they will not produce its like even if some of them were not helpers of others, and even if ... etc. The conjunctive antecedent has been omitted by a regular elision, since the conjoined clause clearly indicates it: if producing its like is negated when they support one another, then it is more fitting that it be negated when they do not. On this point rests the emphasis contained in the concessive "in" and "law," as mentioned more than once. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause, in accordance with what it is conjoined to, i.e., they will not produce its like in any supposed circumstance, even in this circumstance which is contrary to their not producing it, let alone in others. In this there is a cutting off of their vain hopes of wishing to replace some of its verses with others. There is no room for the view that the verse is a confirmation of what precedes it, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then you will not find for yourself against Us any advocate in that regard﴾, as has been said. However, this is not for the reason that has been said, namely that producing its like is harder than retrieving its original, and the negation of a thing is confirmed only by negating what is lesser than it, not what is greater than it. For the difficulty of retrieving it without His command, exalted is He, over producing its like is something beyond doubt. Rather, it is because the oath clause is not directed to the Prophet ﷺ, but to the obstinate deniers before him ﷺ.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 89:

﴿And We have certainly diversified⁠﴾ means: We repeated and reiterated [it] in various modes, which entails greater confirmation and clarification, and a firmer establishment and tranquillity.

﴿for the people in this Qur'an﴾, the Qur'an described by the excellent attributes that have been mentioned.

﴿of every kind of example﴾ means: of every wondrous meaning which is in its beauty and strangeness, and in attracting the soul, like an example, so that they might receive it with acceptance.

﴿but most of the people refused﴾ the explicit noun has been preferred over the pronoun, for emphasis and clarification.

﴿except disbelief﴾ i.e., except denial. The exception from a positive statement is valid here even though "I struck except Zayd" is not valid, because it is interpreted as negative. It is as if it were said: most of them accepted nothing except disbelief. In this there is an emphasis that is not present in "they refused faith", because it indicates that they were not content with any trait other than disbelief in place of faith, hesitation in the matter, and the like; and that they went to great lengths in their non-acceptance, to the point of reaching the rank of outright refusal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 90:

﴿And they said﴾ at the manifestation of their helplessness and the clear overcoming of them by the inimitable Revelation and other dazzling miracles, offering as pretexts things that are not possible to exist in the ordinary course, and whose occurrence wisdom does not require, as is the custom of one who is dumbfounded and refuted.

﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth﴾ It is also read with the doubled (intensive) form (tafjur, taffajur).

﴿For us from the earth﴾ the earth of Makkah, ﴿a spring﴾, a spring whose water never runs dry. Yanbu' is on the pattern yafu'ul, from nabaʿa al-ma' (the water sprang forth), like ya'bub from ʿabba al-ma' (the water surged) when it swells up.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 91:

﴿Or you have a garden﴾ i.e., an orchard whose trees cover what lies beneath them of the open ground, ﴿of palm trees and grapevines, and you cause the rivers to gush forth﴾ i.e., you make them flow forcefully.

﴿Within it, in abundant gushing﴾ abundantly. The meaning is either the channeling of the rivers through it at the time of irrigating it, or the continuous flowing of them, as the "fa'" (fa, "and so") indicates, not the beginning of the flowing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 92:

﴿Or You cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾. *Kisaf* is the plural of *kisfa* (a piece), like *qit'a* and *qit'a* (pieces), in both form (*lafz*) and meaning (*ma'na*). It is also read with a sukun, *kisf*, like *sidra* and *sidr* (lote-tree and lote-trees). It is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "the sky." The *kaf* in *kama* ("as") is in the accusative position (*mahall al-nasb*), as a qualifier (*sifa*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: a falling that is similar to what you claimed (*ightiman mumathilan li-ma za'amta*) (p-195). By this they mean His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or You cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾.

﴿Or You bring God and the angels as a guarantor (*qabilan*)﴾, meaning: as one who confronts (*muqabilan*), like the companion (*'ashir*) and the associate (*mu'ashir*), or as a surety (*kafilan*) who testifies to the truth of what you claim. *Qabilan* is a circumstantial qualifier of "God" (*al-jalala*). The circumstantial qualifier of "the angels" is omitted because it is indicated by the first, meaning: and the angels are guarantors (*qubala'*), just as the predicate is omitted in the line of poetry:

*Fa-inni wa-Qayyarun bi-ha la-gharib*
"Indeed I and Qayyar, in it, are strangers."

Or it is a plural (*jama'a*), so that it is a circumstantial qualifier of "the angels."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 93:

﴿Or you have a house of gold﴾ (zukhruf), i.e., of gold. It has also been read as (bihi), and its origin is "adornment" (zina).

﴿Or you ascend into the sky﴾, i.e., into its ascending paths (ma'arij), the object being elided. One says "ruqqiya fi al-sullam" (he ascended the ladder) and "fi al-darajah" (he ascended the step).

﴿Nor will we believe in your ascent﴾, i.e., for the sake of your ascent alone, or: we will not believe in your ascent into it.

﴿Until you bring down to us a book﴾ from it ﴿that we may read it﴾ ourselves, without it being received from you.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: 'Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said: "We will not believe you until you take a ladder to the sky and climb up on it while I watch, until you reach it and come back with you a sealed document, with four angels accompanying it who bear witness that you are as you say." They did not intend by these vain proposals anything but obstinacy and stubbornness. Even if they had been given many times the signs they proposed, that would only have increased their arrogance. Otherwise, some of the miracles they witnessed, before which the deaf mountains would crumble, would have sufficed them.

﴿Say﴾ (in amazement at the intensity of their obstinacy, and to exalt the sanctuary of the Glorious One above what is hardly fitting for it of such shameful proposals, which the heavens nearly split apart from; or at your request for that, and as an alert to the falsity of what they said): ﴿Glory be to my Lord.﴾ It has also been read as (qala subhana rabbi), ﴿Am I anything but a human being﴾, not an angel, such that ascending into the sky could be imagined from me, and the like.

﴿A messenger﴾, commanded by my Lord to convey the message, without having any choice in the matter, like the rest of the messengers. They would not come to their peoples except with what Allah manifested through their hands, according to what suited the state of their peoples. The matter of signs was not in their hands, nor did they have any right to dictate anything of them to Allah, glory be to Him. His saying "a human being" is the predicate of "kuntu" (I was), and "a messenger" is its attribute.

﴿And what prevented the people﴾, namely those whose falsehoods have been related, ﴿from believing﴾: "that they believe" is the second object of "mana'a" (prevented). The phrase ﴿when the guidance came to them﴾, namely the revelation, is a temporal clause (zarf) governing either "mana'a" or "yu'minu". The sense is: what prevented them, at the time the revelation came accompanied by miracles that called for faith, from believing in the Qur'an and in your prophethood? Or: what prevented them from believing in that at the time the aforementioned came.

﴿Except that they said﴾: this is in the nominative position, as the subject (fa'il) of "mana'a", meaning: except their saying.

﴿Has God sent a mere human as a messenger?﴾ They deny that the Messenger of God, exalted is He, could be of the kind of humans. It is not meant that this statement was made by some of them so that it prevented others from them; rather, the preventing factor is the belief common to all of them, which entails this statement from them. He expressed it as "saying" only to signal that it is a mere saying they utter with their mouths, without any meaning or reality behind it. Limiting the preventer of faith to what has been mentioned, although they have many other obstacles, is because it is the greatest of them, or because it is the actual preventer given the circumstance, namely at the moment of hearing the answer in the words of God Most High: ﴿Say: "I was but a human messenger"﴾, since it is what they then cling to, without any other of their weak doubts coming to mind. This also signals the completeness of their obstinacy, for it indicates that, although the aforementioned answer is decisive in cutting off the roots of their doubts and compelling faith, they reverse the matter and make it an obstacle to faith.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 95:

﴿Say﴾: first, before it, to them, as a clarification of the wisdom and a confirmation of the truth that removes doubt.

﴿If there were﴾: that is, if it existed and settled ﴿in the earth﴾ in place of humankind.

﴿Angels walking about calmly﴾: dwelling in it without ascending to the heaven, and teaching them what needs to be taught.

﴿We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾: guiding them to the truth and directing them to goodness, because they are able to gather and to receive from him. As for ordinary people, they are far from being fit for the angelic mode of address (al-mufawadah al-malakiyyah). And how could they not be? For that depends on likeness and kinship, so sending an angel to them would clash with the wisdom upon which creation and legislation are founded. Rather, an angel is sent from among them only to the elite who are distinguished by pure souls and strengthened by the holy faculty (al-quwwa al-qudsiyya), who are connected to both the spiritual and the physical worlds, so that they may receive from one side and convey to the other.

His saying, exalted is He, "malakan" (an angel), may be a circumstantial accusative (hal) of "rasulan" (a messenger), or it may be a qualifier describing it. The same applies to "basharan" (a human) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ The first possibility is preferred.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 96:

﴿Say﴾ to them a second time, on your own behalf, after you had said to them what you said on Our behalf, and you had explained to them what wisdom requires of the mission, but they did not raise their heads to it.

﴿Allah suffices as a witness﴾ alone ﴿between me and you﴾, that I have discharged the obligations of the message in the most complete manner, and that you have done what you have done of denial, obstinacy, and opposition. The testimony is directed at his ﷺ being a messenger, by manifesting a miracle in accordance with his claim, as chosen (in the preceding discussion); the phrase "between me and you" and what follows of the reasoning does not support this, since it is not "between us" that he said, in order to establish the separation and to make clear the opposition. "Witness" (shahidan) is either a circumstantial accusative (hal) or a specifying accusative (tamyiz).

﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants﴾, from among the messengers and those to whom they were sent, ﴿All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾, encompassing the outward aspects of their conditions and their inward aspects, so He will recompense them for that. This is the reason for the sufficiency, and in it is consolation for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and a threat to the disbelievers.

**﴿And whoever Allah guides﴾** is an independent statement that details what the preceding discourse had alluded to in summary about the recompense of the servants. The meaning is: whoever Allah guides to the truth through the guidance that has come from Him.

**﴿then he is the one guided﴾** to Him, and to the reward that leads to Him, or the one guided to every sought goal.

**﴿And whoever He leads astray﴾**, that is, He creates misguidance in him through his own evil choice, like these obstinate ones.

**﴿then you will not find for them﴾**: the plural pronoun of the group was used, taking into account the meaning of *man* (whoever) after the singular pronoun had been used in its counterpart with regard to its wording. This hints at the oneness of the path of truth and the scarcity of its travellers, and at the multiplicity of the ways of error and the abundance of those who go astray.

**﴿protectors besides Him﴾**, besides Allah, the Exalted, that is, helpers who would guide them to the path of truth, or to a path that would lead them to their worldly and otherworldly aims, or to the path of deliverance from the punishment that their misguidance calls for. The meaning is: you will not find for any one of them a protector, as is required by the correspondence of plural to plural, from the division of the individuals into individuals.

**﴿And We will gather them﴾**: this is a shift (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical person) from the third person to the first person, signifying complete concern with the matter of the gathering.

**﴿on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾** is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the object pronoun, that is: moving upon their faces, being dragged, as in His words: ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces﴾. Or it means walking.

It has been related that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How will they walk upon their faces?" He said: "Indeed, the One who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces."

**﴿blind﴾** is a circumstantial clause referring to the genitive pronoun in the preceding circumstantial clause.

**﴿and dumb and deaf﴾**: they do not see what would gladden their eyes, nor do they speak what would be accepted from them, nor do they hear what would delight their ears. This is because in the world they did not take insight from the signs and lessons, did not speak the truth, and did not listen to it. It is permissible that they be gathered after the reckoning from the place of standing to the Fire with their faculties and senses intact, and that they be gathered thus and then their powers and senses be restored to them, for their perception through these faculties in some situations is beyond doubt.

**﴿Their abode is Hell﴾** is either a circumstantial clause or a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*). Likewise His words: ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾, that is: whenever its flame subsides, by consuming their skins and flesh and no longer leaving in them anything the Fire can take hold of and burn, We increase them in blaze by replacing their skins with other skins, so it returns blazing and flaring. Perhaps this is a punishment for them for their denial of the return after annihilation, by repeating it time after time so that they may see it with their own eyes, since they did not know it through proof, as clarified by His words, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 98:

﴿That﴾ i.e., that punishment.

﴿Their recompense is because they﴾ i.e., because of the fact that they ﴿disbelieved in Our signs﴾, the rational and transmitted ones that clearly indicate the validity of the resurrection (i'adah). So "dhalika" (that) is a subject (mubtada'), and "jaza'uhum" (their recompense) is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for it to be a second subject, with "bi-annahum" (because they) as its predicate, the whole clause being the predicate of "dhalika"; and for "jaza'uhum" to be a substitute (badal) for "dhalika", or an explanatory apposition (bayan) to it, with the predicate being the adverbial phrase (zarf).

﴿And they said﴾, denying in the strongest terms, ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we indeed be raised up as a new creation?"﴾ The phrase "la-mab'uthuna khalqan jadidan" (shall we indeed be raised up as a new creation) is either an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkad) of a verb not from its own root, meaning "shall we indeed be resurrected in a new resurrection"; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "being newly created."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 99:

﴿Do they not see﴾ i.e., do they not reflect and know?

﴿that God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ without any material, despite their immensity, ﴿is able to create the like of them﴾ in smallness; the word "like" (mithl) is superfluous (muqhamm), and what is meant by "creation" is re-creation, as it is expressed by that in the words "a new creation."

﴿And He has appointed for them a term, about which there is no doubt﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "Do they not see," for it has the force of "have they not seen," and the meaning is: they have known that He who is able to create the heavens and the earth is able to create their likes from humankind, and He has appointed for them, and for their resurrection, a definite term about which there is no doubt, namely the Day of Resurrection.

﴿But the wrongdoers refused﴾ The phrase is placed in the position of a pronoun, to record upon them the wrongdoing and their outright transgression of the limit.

﴿except to deny﴾ i.e., obstinate denial.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 100:

﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasures of the mercy of my Lord"﴾ — the treasures of His provision, which He attributed to all existing things. The word "you" (antum) is in the nominative, governed by a verb that is explained by the one mentioned, as in the saying of Hatim: "Even if a woman with bracelets had struck me" (law dhat siwar lataminni). The benefit of this construction is emphasis (al-mubalaghah) and the indication of exclusivity (al-ikhtisas).

﴿Then you would surely withhold﴾ out of your stinginess, ﴿for fear of spending﴾, fearing that it would be exhausted by spending. For there is no one in this world who does not choose benefit for himself; and if he prefers another over himself with something, he prefers it only for a return that exceeds it. Thus he is stingy in comparison with the generosity of God, glorified is He.

﴿And man has always been ever tight-fisted﴾ — excessive in stinginess, because the basis of his affair rests on need, on grudging with what he needs, and on taking into account the return for what he gives.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 101:

﴿And indeed We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾, clear in their indication of his prophethood and of the soundness of what he brought from Allah. They are: the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the flood, the years of drought, and the loss of fruits. It is said that, in place of the last three, they are: the bursting of water from the rock, the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel, and the splitting of the sea. But this is rejected by the fact that these three had not yet been sent down at that time, and that the first two have no connection to Pharaoh, since they were given to the Children of Israel. It is narrated from Safwan ibn 'Assal that "a Jew asked the Prophet ﷺ about them, and he said: Do not associate anything with Him, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not practise sorcery, do not consume usury, do not walk with an innocent man to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not slander a chaste woman, do not flee from the battlefield, and upon you specifically, the Jews, do not transgress on the Sabbath. Then the Jew kissed his hand and his foot ﷺ." Nor does what has been mentioned support this either. Perhaps his ﷺ answer with this was because it was what mattered most to the questioner, and his acceptance of it was because it was written in the Torah; and he knew that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had only known it through revelation.

﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. It is also read as (fa-sal), meaning: We said to him, "Ask them about Pharaoh, and say to him, 'Send with me the Children of Israel'," or "Ask them about their faith," or "about the condition of their religion." Or, "Ask them to support you." This is supported by the reading of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the past tense form. It is also said that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: ask them about those signs so that you may increase in certainty and tranquillity, or so that your truthfulness may become manifest.

﴿When he came to them﴾ is connected to "We said" and to "ask" under the mentioned reading, and to "Our signs", or to an implied verb, "they informed you", or to "mention", if the address is to the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿Pharaoh said to him﴾. The "fa" (in "fa-qala") is an elliptical connective (fa-sihah), meaning: so he displayed before Pharaoh the clear signs We had given him, and conveyed to him what he had been sent with, and Pharaoh said to him:

﴿Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched.﴾ You have been bewitched, so your mind has become confused.

﴿He said: "You certainly know that none has sent these down"﴾, meaning the signs that he displayed.

﴿except the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, their Creator and their Governor (mudabbir). The mention of His lordship (rububiyyah) over them indicates that none is able to bring forth signs so great except their Creator and their Governor.

﴿as clear proofs﴾: this is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) of "the signs", meaning: as manifest proofs that make you see my truthfulness, but you are obstinate and arrogant. Like the verse, "And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them." It follows from that knowledge that he (ﷺ) was in perfect soundness of mind, let alone the supposition of being bewitched. It was also read as ʿalimtu (عَلِمْتُ) in the first-person form, meaning: "I have certainly known with conviction that these dazzling signs were sent down by God, may His authority be exalted, so how can it be supposed that magic could hover around me?"

﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed.﴾ Mathbūr means turned away from good and inclined toward evil, from their saying: "What has turned you (ṣarafaka) away from this?" (mā thabaraka ʿan hādhā), i.e., what has diverted you. Or it means destroyed. Moses (ﷺ) countered his assumption with his own assumption, and how different the two are. How could they not be? Pharaoh's assumption (p-199) "Indeed, you are clearly…", and his (ﷺ) assumption borders on certainty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 103:

﴿So he intended﴾, that is, Pharaoh, ﴿to drive them﴾, that is, to make them light (yastakhiffahum) and to unsettle them, ﴿out of the land﴾, the land of Egypt, or out of the land in general by killing, like His saying: ﴿We will slay their sons and spare their women﴾.

﴿Then We drowned him and those with him, all of them﴾. So We turned his scheming back upon him, and We made him and his people light (istafazzanahu) by drowning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 104:

﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land"﴾ after their drowning, ﴿the land from which he intended to drive you out﴾, ﴿and when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ the final return (karra al-akhira), or the life (al-hayah), or the Hour (al-sa'ah), and the Last Abode (al-dar al-akhira), that is, the establishment of the Resurrection, ﴿We will bring you together in a mingled throng﴾, mixed together, you and them, ﴿then We will judge among you and distinguish your blessed from your wretched.﴾ Al-lafif (throng) means groups from various tribes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 105:

﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended.﴾ That is: We did not send down the Qur'an except as conjoined with the truth that necessitated its sending down, and it did not descend except as conjoined with the truth that it contains. Or: We did not send it down from the heaven except as preserved, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except as preserved from the confusion of the devils. Perhaps the intended meaning is to explain that falsehood does not afflict it, neither at the beginning of the matter nor at its end.

﴿And We did not send you except as a bringer of good news﴾ to the obedient, of reward,

﴿and a warner﴾ to the disobedient, of punishment. This is a confirmation of the truth of the Prophet's mission (ﷺ) following the confirmation of the truth of the sending down of the Qur'an.

**Qur'an 17:106**

﴿And a Qur'an﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb which is explained by His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have separated it﴾. It is also read with the doubled consonant (tashdid), indicating the great number of its installments (nujum).

﴿So that you may recite it to the people at a deliberate pace (ʿala mukth)﴾: at leisure and with deliberation. For that is easier for memorization and more helpful for understanding. It is also read with a fatha (ʿala maktin), which is a dialectal variant of it.

﴿And We have sent it down in gradual revelation (tanzil)﴾: in accordance with what wisdom and benefit require, and in keeping with the events and occurrences that take place.

Say (to those who disbelieve): "Believe in it or do not believe in it." Your belief does not add to its perfection, and your refusal does not diminish it.

Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it: that is, the scholars who read the earlier books before its revelation, who knew the reality of revelation and the signs of prophethood, who were able to distinguish truth from falsehood and the one who is right from the one who is wrong, and who saw in those books your description and the description of what was sent down to you.

When it is recited: that is, the Qur'an.

upon them, they fall: that is, they fall upon their faces.

prostrating: out of glorification of God's command, or in thanks for the fulfilment of what was promised in those books concerning your being sent. The mention of the chins is to indicate complete humility, since falling down upon them is then realized. The choice of the preposition "li" (for/to) is to indicate that the falling is specifically upon them, as in the verse:

*So he fell prone, for the two hands and for the mouth.*

This is a justification (ta'lil, an explanation of the cause) for what is understood from God's words "Believe in it or do not believe" regarding the lack of concern for that. That is: if you do not believe in it, then one who is better than you has believed in it in the best manner of belief. It may also be a justification for "Say" by way of consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as if it were said: "Be consoled by the belief of the scholars concerning the belief of the ignorant, and do not be concerned with their belief or their turning away."

(p-200) ﴿And they say﴾ in their prostration, ﴿Glory be to our Lord﴾ (exalted is our Lord) above what the disbelievers do of denial, or above breaking His promise.

﴿Indeed, the promise of our Lord has certainly been fulfilled﴾. "Inna" is a lightened form of the heavy "inna" (in-na, "indeed"), and the "lam" is the lam that distinguishes it from negation; i.e., the matter is indeed this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 109:

﴿And they fall down on their faces weeping﴾. He repeated "falling down upon the chins" because the causes differ. The first is for the glorification of God Most High's command, or in thanks for the fulfilment of His promise. The second is because of what the admonitions of the Qur'an had affected in them, while they were weeping out of fear of God.

﴿And it increases them﴾, i.e., the Qur'an increases them, by their hearing it,

﴿in humility﴾, just as it increases them in knowledge and certainty of God Most High.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 110:

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful.﴾ It was revealed when the polytheists heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, O Most Merciful." They said: "He forbids us to worship two gods, yet he calls upon another god." The Jews said: "You make little mention of the Most Merciful, while Allah the Exalted has made much mention of Him in the Torah."

The meaning according to the first view is that the two names are equivalent, being expressions for one and the same essence, even though the aspects of meaning differ, and that the affirmation of divine oneness (tawhid) pertains only to the essence that is worshipped. According to the second view, the two names are equal in the goodness of their use and in leading to the intended purpose. This second view better accords with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ The word "calling" (du'a') here means "naming" (tasmiyah), and it takes two objects, the first of which has been omitted as being understood. "Or" (aw) here indicates choice (takhyir). The tanwin in "ayyan" is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted (al-mudaf ilayhi). The particle "ma" is added to emphasize the indefiniteness contained in "ayy". The pronoun in "lahu" refers to the One named (al-musamma), because the naming belongs to Him and not to the name. The original structure of the statement was "Whichever you call upon, it is good," so it was replaced with "to Him belong the most beautiful names," for emphasis and to indicate what the proof is for. Since the goodness of all His names requires the goodness of those two names. As for their being "most beautiful," it is because they indicate the attributes of perfection: majesty, beauty and generosity.

﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾, that is, in the recitation of your prayer such that the polytheists hear it, for that would lead them to revile and to engage in vain talk during it. ﴿Nor be silent in it﴾, that is, in its recitation such that those behind you among the believers do not hear it.

﴿And seek a way between those﴾, that is, between loudness and silence in the manner mentioned.

﴿A way﴾, a moderate, balanced course, for the best of matters are their middle. The expression of this as "a way" is by consideration that it is a matter to which those who turn toward it direct themselves, which those who follow take as their aim, and which conveys them to the desired goal. It is narrated that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) used to speak in a low voice and would say: "I converse with my Lord, and He knows my need." And 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to speak loudly and would say: "I drive away Satan and wake the drowsy." When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered Abu Bakr to raise his voice slightly, and 'Umar to lower his voice slightly. It has been said: the meaning is, do not be loud in all of your prayer, nor be silent in all of it, but seek a way between them, by being silent during the day and loud at night. It has also been said: "your prayer" here means "your supplication." A group held that it was abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 17, verse 111:

(p-201) ﴿And say: "Praise be to Allah, who has not taken a son,"﴾ as the Jews, the Christians, and the Banu Maliy claim, where they said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," "al-Masih is the son of Allah," and "the angels are the daughters of Allah." Allah is exalted far above that, with a great exaltation.

﴿And He has no partner in dominion,﴾ that is, in divinity, as the Thanawiyya (Dualists) say, those who affirm a plurality of gods. ﴿Nor has He any protector out of weakness,﴾ that is, no helper, and none who prevents harm from Him by virtue of his might; or, He does not take anyone as an ally because of some humiliation that he seeks to ward off through him. The mention, in the midst of the praise, of these sublime attributes indicates that the one deserving of praise is the one whose attributes these are, and no other, for through them perfection is complete, along with complete power to originate, and what follows from it of bestowing various kinds of blessings. Whatever else there is, is deficient, owned, its blessing bestowed, or one upon whom blessing is bestowed. For this reason, the Exalted's words are joined to it: ﴿And magnify Him with full magnification.﴾ In this is an admonition that the servant, however much he exceeds in glorifying and extolling God, and strives in obedience and praise, should acknowledge his shortcoming. Concerning this, it is narrated that when a boy from the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib became articulate, the Prophet (ﷺ) would teach him this noble verse.

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat Bani Isra'il and his heart softens at the mention of the two parents, he will have a qintar in Paradise." The qintar is one thousand two hundred ounces.

And praise belongs to Allah, glory be to Him, and to Him belong majesty, greatness, and omnipotence.
